#9060. Exhibition as Living Archive: the 1950s Baghdad Modern Art Group in the UAE Today

All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group, Curated by Nada Shabout, on view at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery through January 3, 2027

The Baghdad Modern Art Group was established in 1951 by two of Iraq’s most influential artists, Jewad Selim (1919–1961) and Shakir Hassan Al Said (1925–2004), and grew to engage many of Iraq’s leading artists, architects, poets, and more. Together, they sought to develop a new art form, one that negotiated a time of globally inflected modernism from Baghdad, an Abbasid city (est. 762 CE) that traces its lineage to the ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia. In All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group at NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Dr. Nada Shabout brings together the artists from this circle, as well as those whom its work influenced, both at the time and in the following generations, until today.

After the Kingdom of Iraq’s formation in 1932 as an independent state, Iraqi artists explored the new parameters of the secularized, modern society that was emerging following Britain’s maneuvering to dismantle the Ottoman Empire. Artists questioned the ability of traditional “Islamic art” practices to present their contemporary realities, searching for a more effective visual language. In this context, modern art provided a conduit for exploration and was perceived by Iraqi artists as a global space of shared humanity.

Various artist groups launched initiatives to convey the importance of national representation through culture, which included promoting the modern art movement in Iraq. This period set the stage for Iraq’s so-called golden age of the 1950s: a time of maturation for a generation of artists pivotal in initiating rigorous standards of art theory and practice, thus charting new possibilities for future generations.

The experimental ethos of the group continues to resonate today beyond Baghdad to direct and connect contemporary Iraqi artists around the world to each other.

Featured artists include Faraj Abbo, Sadik Kwaish Alfraji, Himat Mohammad Ali, Rasoul Alwan, Suad al-Attar, Qahtan Awni, Dia al-Azzawi, Bogus Bablanian, Amar Dawod, Ghassan Ghaib, Faiq (Faeq) Hassan, Mohammed Ghani Hikmat, Jabra Ibrahim Jabra, Rand Abdul Jabbar, Fouad Jihad, Saadi Al Kaabi, Ardash Kakafian, Salma Khoury, Hanaa Malallah, Mahmoud Obaidi, Widad al-Orfali, Khalid al-Rahal, Kareem Risan, Miran al-Saadi, Mahmoud Sabri, Naziha Salim, Nizar (Nazar) Salim, Shakir Hassan Al Said, Delair Shaker, Jewad Selim, Lorna Selim, Walid Siti, Ismail Fattah (Al-Turk), Madiha Umar, Khalil al-Ward, and Nazar Yahya.

The exhibition’s curator Dr. Nada Shabout has published widely on modern and contemporary Arab and Iraqi art and has curated numerous exhibitions. She has joined NYU Abu Dhabi as a senior investigator at al Mawrid Arab Center for the Study of Art and as a visiting professor of art history. She is the founding president of the Association for Modern and Contemporary Art from the Arab World, Iran, and Turkey (AMCA) and founding director of the Modern Art Iraq Archive (MAIA).

The exhibition is on view at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery through January 3, 2027.

“He embraced people wholeheartedly, recognized what they needed, and connected them with opportunities and with one another,” said Calvillo’s colleague.

Fernando Calvillo, an esteemed artist and leader in Oklahoma City's arts community, died in a high-speed collision between two trains in the province of Toledo, Spain, on Wednesday, October 28. #9058. Former High Museum of Art executive sentenced to 12 months in prison for embezzlement

Auguste Rodin's The Shade at the High Museum of Art, Atlanta Photo: Marc Merlin, via Flickr

Brady Lum, a former chief operating officer at Atlanta's High Museum of Art, was sentenced to 12 months in federal prison on Monday (2 November) for embezzling more than $600,000 from the institution. The sentencing comes as the High celebrates its centennial and its parent organisation, the Woodruff Arts Center, conducts a major corporate fundraising campaign.

Federal prosecutors said Lum diverted museum funds to pay for personal purchases, including guitars, music lessons and woodworking equipment. He concealed the expenditures through falsified invoices, reimbursement requests and accounting adjustments. The scheme began in September 2019, less than nine months after Lum joined the museum, and continued until its discovery in November 2025.

Lum paid full restitution of $607,688.18 to the High and voluntarily paid approximately $500,000 more to cover costs the museum incurred while uncovering and investigating his criminal activity.

During Monday's hearing, US District judge Michael L. Brown focused extensively on the deterrent purpose of sentencing. Although Brown said he did not believe Lum was likely to reoffend, he emphasised the court's responsibility to discourage similar financial crimes by others in positions of trust.

The judge acknowledged similarities between his own professional and socioeconomic background and Lum's, discussing how sentencing structures have historically been shaped by educated, professionally successful individuals whose circumstances resemble those of many white-collar defendants.

Brown also considered Lum's prompt restitution after the misconduct was discovered, distinguishing between voluntarily returning stolen funds before detection and repaying them after being caught. The latter, he indicated, carried less weight in assessing accountability.

Lum addressed the court and apologised for his conduct, expressing regret for disappointing his family and community. The gallery appeared to consist largely of relatives, friends and supporters of Lum.

Contacted for comment following Monday's sentencing, a spokesperson for the Woodruff provided the following statement: "We respect the court’s decision and remain focused on fulfilling our mission, responsibly managing our resources and connecting deeply with the audience we serve."

Both the Woodruff and the High declined to provide substantive information about financial safeguards introduced following Lum's misconduct, or whether they intend to publish a remediation plan addressing financial controls, governance reforms and oversight procedures.

#9057. The Art of Showing Up

Voting stickers adorn memorials to ICE victims, Jeremy Shaw talks grief and ecstasy, and a portable archive of East LA.

It was raining like crazy when I cast my vote yesterday in Iowa, a blood-red state so battered, beleaguered, and embittered by an affordability crisis and farm debt and crumbling infrastructure that it just might — just might — swing. It’d been a steady stream all day, a poll worker told me, and she didn’t mean the rain.

The vox populi doesn’t just speak from the ballot box. In Houston, for instance, a memorial’s been talking: Dozens of “I Voted” stickers now adorn a roadside tribute to Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a man ICE murdered in July, in an impromptu participatory artwork that is now being echoed in shrines to others around the country. “I voted for you,” someone wrote.

It makes me think of the ways we make ourselves heard, the ways we honor one another. The day after a deadly attack on Berlin’s Pride Festival this summer, about 200 people gathered at Jeremy Shaw’s video installation of dancers moving toward ecstatic revelation, he told writer Eileen G’Sell in a profile today, turning the gallery into a space of collective mourning, defiance, and solidarity. And a new project by Guadalupe Rosales, writes Carolina A. Miranda, is a tribute to her Eastside Los Angeles upbringing, and to the friends and relationships that offered a respite from rising violence and anti-immigrant sentiment. It’s what we do — create meaning, build a community, find a way forward.

Last month, Paul Ramírez Jonas invited the people of Toronto to sit down with a stranger in a public space, make a promise, swear on it, see it spelled out on a large-scale marquee, and then memorialize it in a one-of-a-kind contract they kept. One of hundreds of such vows was: “I promise to disagree better.” | Anna Gallagher-Ross and Kate Gilbert

The clever campaign presents the 'Ultimate Monster Costume'.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Halloween 2026 saw some creepy get ups. Many of the most striking were highly elaborate, including Heidi Klum as a bloody severed hand, Neil Patrick Harris and David Burtka as the Grady twins and Alexis Stone dressing as Michael Jackson.

But could the creepiest Halloween costume of the year be something a lot more prosaic? A clever creative campaign hit hard over the spooky season by arguing that 'the ultimate monster costume' involves little effort and could just as easily be worn on any other day of the year.

On the surface, the social campaign was designed to look like a retail ad for an online Halloween costume store. But clicking through leads to a website listing what's described as a 'Real Life Monster Costume': an intentionally average men's white T-shirt and jeans with white trainers.

While, the costume immediately stands out for its apparent mundaneness, things take a turn in the description of what it includes. the site lists: friend/classmate/boyfriend/colleague/husband and outfit features: invading women’s personal space/ sharing nudes without consent/visiting chat rooms for tips on drugging.

The copy on the ‘buy’ button says 'DON’T BUY THIS BEHAVIOUR'.

A post shared by Ultimate Monsters (@ultimate_monsters)

The Ultimate Monster Costume was a tactical social campaign from Do Not Behave, an independent UK-based creative studio founded by creative director Jo Moore last year. The agency teamed up with educators What Makes a Man and Cheer Up Luv.

The aim of the unusual and paradoxically eye-catching ad was to highlight issues around violence against women and girls. The campaign suggests that the monsters behind sexual violence are often hard to detect because they often look like "everyday guys". Do Not Behave said it had received over 2.5k visits to the spoof site.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The agency notes that violence against women and girls is being treated as a national emergency in the UK, with studies showing that it impacts roughly one in 12 women in England and Wales, taking the form of domestic abuse, sexual assault and rape, stalking, harassment, forced marriage, female genital mutilation, and digital/online abuse.

According to the Women and Girls Network, research indicates that approximately 97% of women who report sexual assault know their attacker. The campaign found a clever way to raise awareness of how commonplace the issue can be, particularly aiming get the attention of other men to ask male allies to be more vigilant.

#9054. "If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly"

Architects are increasingly, and existentially, anxious about AI. It can already produce images, generate endless options, manipulate form, draft text, analyse information and take on increasing amounts of technical production. The predictable professional response is to become defensive: to identify the bits of architectural work that machines cannot yet do, protect them, regulate them and insist ever more loudly on the special status of the architect.

This is absolutely the wrong response. Architecture has always had a tendency to retreat when it feels threatened: as its actual control over the production of buildings has diminished, it has clung ever more tightly to authorship, professional territory and the idea that certain activities somehow belong uniquely to architects. AI merely makes the weakness of that position more visible.

If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly. If producing drawings, images, options and information constitutes our entire claim to value, we are defining our value in far too limited terms.

We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers

The profession has spent decades confusing the production of architectural artefacts with architectural intelligence, and we have run out of road. We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers. If we design a back extension, give it a sufficiently enigmatic name, photograph it carefully, attach enough rhetoric, we somehow persuade ourselves that we have made Ronchamp.

Architectural culture has encouraged this inflation for decades, in that every modest building becomes a manifesto, every detail becomes a proposition and every project arrives with the expectation that it should reveal something profound about architecture itself.

But the age of the hero is exhausted. The profession no longer has the cultural authority, the economic power or, frankly, the public attention to sustain this fantasy, however enthusiastically we continue to perform it for one another. AI may simply accelerate the reckoning: if machines can generate endless formal novelty and beautiful images, the architect’s claim to importance can’t continue to rest on being the singular creative intelligence who produces the special object.

Click here to read more about the issues facing architecture in our Performance Review series.

The economic model that supported this fantasy is broken too. Architecture remains notoriously poorly paid relative to the length and cost of its education, the responsibility it carries and the hours it routinely demands. Yet architects have tolerated this for decades because the profession offered another form of compensation – the most important thing of all for architects: recognition, via awards, publications, photographs, lectures, the approval of our peers and the possibility that one small project might provide a tiny share of architectural glory.

We have accepted low pay, long hours, insecure employment and unpaid competitions partly because we have been sold the idea that authorship itself is a reward. If the work is meaningful enough, beautiful enough or visible enough, perhaps the sacrifice will somehow be justified.

That bargain has always been dubious, but it now looks increasingly absurd. Most architects will never become Corbusier, however many evenings they work, and most projects will never become Ronchamp, however much rhetoric is wrapped around them. Architectural status – irrelevant to most outside a handful of people in the profession – has nevertheless become a kind of substitute currency, and architecture has been remarkably successful at persuading people to accept less of the real kind in return.

We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do

AI makes the bargain even harder to sustain. If the production work on which fees have traditionally depended becomes faster and cheaper, defending the same exhausted model will simply drive fees and salaries down further.

The answer cannot be to produce the same things more efficiently for less money. We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do.

The more interesting response to AI is not to ask how architects protect what they currently do, but what architects might become capable of doing if some of that work no longer defines them.

With this, architectural intelligence becomes most useful where there is no simple answer. The most interesting projects rarely arrive as neatly defined problems awaiting visually arresting solutions. Instead, they involve conflicting needs, uncertain briefs, difficult sites, volatile markets, limited resources, political constraints and people who want different things. They involve other consultants who know things the architect does not, clients who change their minds, communities whose needs cannot be compressed into a consultation report and materials that stubbornly refuse to behave predictably like lines on a drawing.

This mess is the essence of architecture. The most useful architect is not simply the person who generates a solution, they are someone able to enter an unresolved situation, figure out what the problem actually is, connect different forms of knowledge, make spatial judgements and establish enough structure for something useful to emerge via collective endeavour rather than their own brilliance.

This demands a radically different model of authorship, which is less author and more host. That doesn’t mean becoming a passive facilitator, it means knowing how to bring people together, anticipating problems, establish frameworks within which others can work, exercising judgement, knowing when to intervene, and knowing when to shut up and not be the hero.

It also changes what architects might reasonably be paid for. At present, architecture fees are overwhelmingly organised around a relatively linear journey from brief, to concept, to information, to construction and eventually completion, but much of the work that might make architecture genuinely valuable sits awkwardly around the edges of that process.

Understanding a problem before a brief becomes fixed is often unpaid. Working seriously with communities gets compressed into consultation. Engaging directly with materials and makers is treated as secondary to design. Returning after occupation to understand what worked and what failed is rarely properly funded. Helping a building adapt over years barely appears in conventional fee structures at all.

There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like

But architects should be paid for diagnosis and briefing, for bringing different forms of knowledge together, for testing possibilities at full scale, negotiating spatial conflicts, post-occupancy work, adaptation and long-term stewardship. Practices should be able to maintain relationships with buildings and communities rather than disappearing at practical completion. Architecture fees might begin to pay for judgement over time, rather than simply production on the way towards an object.

This is not some romantic idea of architects becoming artists, activists or community workers instead of running viable businesses (which contemporary practice is not). Quite the opposite: it is about identifying forms of architectural value that are difficult to automate and, more importantly, are actually useful.

For the past 20 years, our educational initiative Studio in the Woods (pictured top and left) has accidentally provided a small laboratory for some of this. Its significance has never really been the timber structures that emerge over several days of co-production. Instead, the interesting aspect of Studio in the Woods is what happens when people design and make together under conditions in which the answer is not known beforehand, where ideas encounter the friction of weight, resistance, gravity, tools and materials. Where experts and non-experts work together as equals, and leadership moves according to what needs to happen next.

The skill of the architect in these situations is not to surrender judgement, but to exercise it differently. What should be negotiated? What can remain unresolved? Where is precision necessary? Where might uncertainty be productive? Who knows something that I do not? These are much more interesting questions for the future of the profession than whether AI can draw a convincing building.

There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like: eliminating uncertainty, standardising processes, increasing predictability, producing ever-more information and pretending that buildings can be completely resolved before anybody actually makes them. Now, machines are becoming extremely capable at exactly those things and we are surprised to find ourselves threatened, and we should stop trying to beat them at their own game.

Human architectural intelligence is at its richest when it is situated, relational and embodied. It involves judgement without complete information and responsibility for consequences that cannot be fully predicted. It means understanding materials as part of landscapes and economies, buildings as things that change through occupation, and design as something produced between many people rather than delivered by one.

None of this means drawings, technical knowledge, form or aesthetic judgement cease to matter. They matter enormously, but they are merely parts of architectural intelligence, not its definition.

The architect of the future does not need to be the person with the most original idea and the most charisma. They might instead be the person who can understand an uncertain situation, recognise what matters, establish a framework for action and create the conditions in which something richer than their own initial idea can emerge. AI may make the old version of the architect less necessary, but I’m not sure that is something we should mourn.

Piers Taylor is the founder of architecture practice Invisible Studio and the convenor of Studio in the Woods. He is professor of knowledge exchange in architecture at the University of the West of England and an external examiner at the Arts University Bournemouth, having previously held positions with the Architectural Association and the University of Cambridge. He holds a PhD from the University of Reading. He has presented several architecture shows on television including BBC programmes The House that £100k Built and The World’s Most Extraordinary Homes. His first book, Learning from the Local, was published in 2025.

#9053. Doris Salcedo on Colombia's Refusal to Forget

“Works of art last much longer than their governments,” she told Hyperallergic in an interview following the far-right president’s removal of works from the National Museum.

On October 15, dozens of objects were removed from display at the Museo Nacional in Bogotá under the orders of the country’s far-right president, Abelardo De la Espriella. Among them were artworks and materials related to LGBTQ+ and feminist movements; the country's 2016 peace agreement with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC); and the campaigns of left-wing leaders Carlos Pizarro and Bernardo Jaramillo Ossa, both assassinated in the 1990s, whom De la Espriella has called “terrorists.” The objects were reinstated within two weeks by a court order, but the incident roiled the nation: Hundreds took to the streets in protest and faced police repression.

In the days that followed, I called Doris Salcedo. The last time we spoke was in 2021, when her installation-space “Fragmentos” in Bogotá — an “anti-monument” marking the end of Colombia's bloody guerrilla war, with a floor made of melted-down FARC weapons shaped by women who suffered assault during the conflict — had been usurped by conservative populist president Iván Duque. Now, in a different but hauntingly resonant context of state-sanctioned erasure, I turned to Salcedo to help make sense of this moment.

The Colombian artist has made a practice of memory. Her deeply poetic works, comprising both intimate sculpture and expansive, site-specific public interventions, exist at the intersection of historical trauma, mourning, and tribute. They conjure the victims of political violence and disappearance not by simply remembering or looking back, but by delicately articulating the contours of their absence.

Salcedo and I spoke ahead of her trip to New York, where she is presenting new works at White Cube gallery on November 13. She shared characteristically elegant reflections on Colombia’s pain, its echoes in the present, and the country's legacy of political art: “They know they are going to be portrayed,” she said, in a pointed reminder to those in power, “and that works of art last much longer than their governments.”

Our conversation, published in both English and the original Spanish below, has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Hyperallergic: Hi, Doris. It’s a pleasure to hear you. You know, when I emailed you, I thought: I can’t believe it’s been five years since we last spoke. And now, writing to you again, in this context ... Is everything okay with you, all things considered?

Doris Salcedo: Yes, what a complex moment. Well, let’s see, it’s very difficult to live under an authoritarian government that moves very quickly. That is, in two months it has destroyed what Trump took two years to destroy. Colombian society reacts in unusual ways. And of all the scandals, of all the consensuses this president has broken, for some reason that is hard to understand, this act of censorship at the Museo Nacional is the one that has been most publicized and the one that has provoked the most widespread anger. That is, a series of extremely serious events has occurred, but society has not mobilized and has not raised its voice. In this case, it has.

H: I was thinking of what’s happening in the United States with Trump and the Smithsonian. Generally speaking, people here haven’t mobilized significantly in response to Trump’s crackdown on museums. But in Latin America, it seems people feel very attacked when governments touch art and culture.

DS: Yes, because it’s censorship. I don’t know if it’s because of the history of repression we carry with us, because we’ve already lived through it, because we already know what it’s like. And maybe because young people feel very threatened. But the reaction has been beautiful, moving, strong. Young professors from different universities took their classes to the steps in front of the museum and taught there, in the street, in front of the museum. This happened on October 15, and since that day, every single day we’ve had people in front of the museum. It’s a very beautiful and very moving thing.

H: How fantastic! That space is being activated in an incredible way, the complete opposite of what the government intended.

DS: It’s a bit curious, because the Museo Nacional was a museum that for quite a few years, not only under this administration but under previous ones, particularly the last one, was very badly run. It had poor leadership, with poor programming, and it was a somewhat lackluster museum. And now, this act of censorship brings it into the light. Seeing those square rectangles, those ghostly rectangles with a little dust, where the paintings have been removed ... those absences become an extremely powerful presence. People have reproduced the paintings and the objects taken out of the collection, and those reproductions are displayed at the museum’s door. That is, this act of censorship gave enormous fertility to the cultural world, which reacted in an intelligent and creative way.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#9051. Claire Valdez Will Be Your Artist in Congress

The artist, former cultural worker, and union organizer won a seat in the US House of Representatives by nearly 70 percentage points.

Among the historic wave of triumphs for Democrats in yesterday's midterms, New York State Assemblywoman Claire Valdez, an artist, former cultural worker, and union organizer, was elected to represent New York's 7th Congressional District in the United States House of Representatives.

After a resounding win in the June primary, the 37-year-old Democratic Socialist will represent the so-called "Commie Corridor," a district encompassing north Brooklyn and western Queens that also overwhelmingly voted for Valdez's endorser, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, last November. She defeated her opponent, Republican Melvin Rivera, by 68 percentage points, and will succeed retiring Democratic Representative Nydia Velázquez, who has held the seat since 2013.

Central to Valdez's campaign were measures aimed at protecting unions and workers' rights, and addressing the affordability crisis.

"As somebody who once aspired to be an artist and came to New York to pursue that dream, the purpose of our movement is to make sure that anyone can be an artist, that everyone has the time off, and the living wages, and the healthcare, and the space to pursue passions, to spend time with family, to live a good life," Valdez told Hyperallergic Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara in an interview in June this year.

#9050. Minimalist House in Japan by FORM/Kouichi Kimura is "reduced to the essentials"

A monochrome palette and pared-back, open interiors define the aptly named Minimalist House, a home in Japan designed by local studio FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects.

Located in Shiga prefecture, the 73-square-metre home is formed of cubic volumes clad in corrugated metal and black render, perched on a hill overlooking the nearby Lake Biwa.

Minimalist House was designed for a single occupant, but FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects wanted to challenge the assumption that this would mean small-feeling interiors.

This led the studio to create a series of voids and long sightlines that it said help to “liberate space”.

“When hearing ‘a home for a single occupant’, people typically imagine a compact house,” founder Kouichi Kimura told Dezeen.

“Here, living alone is regarded not as a spatial constraint, but as a condition that liberates space,” he added.

“Starting from the individual as the base unit, the house explores a new way of single-person living through the minimal composition reduced to the essentials, with the space that invites in the surrounding view, light, wind, and sound.”

The plan of Minimalist House revolves around a tall void cut through its centre, which extends upwards into a skinny, double-height volume projecting from its roof with a large window.

Finished with grey-plastered walls and dark stone floors, a kitchen, dining space and study occupy the ground floor, with metal and concrete steps leading up to a living space and bedroom above.

Facing the road, the front of the home has been left almost entirely blank. Instead, the interiors open up on the opposite side towards views of the lake in the distance, with the dining table, study and bed pushed up against large, deep-set windows.

“Each floor is designed as a single open layout,” explained Kimura. “The double-height space vertically connects the upper and lower levels. Manipulating floor and ceiling levels gently articulates each space without clearly dividing them.”

“The living space on the upper level is designed not only for daily life, but also for enjoying music. Within the double-height volume, sound resonates off the walls and ceiling, filling the entire space,” he added.

A glass corridor with sliding doors separates the main home from a single-storey washroom, which the studio introduced to ensure that this everyday passage would capture views out over the lake.

“Placing these wet areas away from the main structure creates a natural flow of movement in daily life,” Kimura explained.

“Walking through the glazed corridor in between allows one to touch the landscape, light, and breeze, offering a gentle transition in the everyday time,” he added.

Minimalist forms and interiors often feature in the work of FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects, with the studio’s previous projects in Shiga including a blocky hair salon and home and a skinny home with carefully-placed windows to avoid overlooking.

#9049. November Book Bag: from a book about broken art to a collection of Zanele Muholi’s LGBTQ+ portraits

This ancient Greek Colossal Head of a Youth (around 200BC-100BC) features in The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture Antikensammlung, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, inv. AvPVII 283. bpk Bildagentur / Antikensammlung/Staatliche Museen zu Berlin / Ingrid Geske / Art Resource, NY

The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture explores the enduring fascination with fractured statues, focusing on the “power dynamics of iconoclastic dismantling and defacement, and how various cultures treat broken statues”, says a publisher’s statement. Highlights include Michelangelo’s terracotta Model of a Nude Woman (around 1533), which new research suggests may have been intentionally created incomplete. The publication accompanies a wide-ranging and eclectic exhibition spanning more than 4,500 years of global history, which opened in September at the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence before it travels to the National Gallery of Art in Washington DC next year.

This newly revised and expanded edition assesses the relevance today of the influential conceptual artist Felix Gonzalez-Torres who died from an Aids-related illness in 1996. “Almost two decades after its original publication, the monograph accompanying Gonzalez-Torres’s 1995 retrospective at the Guggenheim Museum is still the canonical text on the artist,” says a publisher’s statement. Gonzalez-Torres is known especially for his famous sweet installations, which are usually mounted in piles in the corner of rooms. “The candy pieces, like all his works, encourage a wealth of meanings, and can be everything from stridently political to gently lyrical,” writes the critic and host of The Art Newspaper’s podcast, Ben Luke.

This publication grew out of a video project devised by the cultural producer Gabriela Galcerán in which 26 artists chose a word, one for each letter of the alphabet, and responded to it in their own way. The five thematic chapters, including “Power + Politics” and “Agency + Language”, subsequently draw connections between their ideas. Contributors include Lynn Hershman Leeson, Lawrence Abu Hamdan and Gary Hill. “They all made me flinch, each for a different reason. I love the wide range of tones and registers that make up this choral effort. Some are intimate, some political, some humorous or oblique,” says Galcerán in a statement.

For more than 20 years, the South African artist and activist Zanele Muholi has been documenting Black lesbian and bisexual women, along with queer, trans, non-binary, and gender fluid people for the project Faces and Phases. This new volume of the work, released to mark the project’s 20th anniversary, has been updated to include new sitters in locations such as São Paulo, Salvador, London, Porto and Los Angeles. “These striking photographs are often accompanied by participants’ testimonies, sharing their personal stories, feelings, and lived experiences,” says a publisher’s statement. Muholi was born in Durban in 1972 at the height of apartheid in South Africa. In the early 2000s, the photographer began to raise awareness of the hypocrisies and hate crimes that remain prevalent against the LGBTQ+ community within the country.

Simulation hands the hard work of moving objects over to maths, physics and a little chaos.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This is a part of our series of features on the basics of 3D art and animation. You might want to see the previous pieces on 3D art workflows, what a 3D object is made of, how to smooth or harden 3D models and the importance of pivots and centre points.

If you need the tools to get started, see our guides to the best 3D modelling software.

Animating a single metal ball bouncing down a staircase is a relatively simple animation which can be done by keyframing. Animating 100 metal balls down a staircase is anything but relatively simple. Animating a window opening, again simple to keyframe; animating the curtains of the window blowing in the breeze, potentially complicated.

This is what simulations are for, and it’s the same when animating liquid, or fire and smoke. Many 3D applications offer the ability to create at least hard (the bouncing metal balls) or soft body simulations (the curtains blowing in the wind), while some offer a full simulation suite which will include particle and fluid simulations.

The trade-off is control. A hand keyed animation does allow the artist to have full control of every single aspect of the animation and finesse a move, artistically, every time. A simulation does what the physics decides (which admittedly the artist has control of), but this can mean an iterative workflow of experiments of allowing the simulation to calculate the moves, the artist to review, and then go again.

Most 3D applications let you ‘bake’ a simulation once you’re happy, freezing the result into ordinary keyframes you can still tweak and play back more easily, but the physics would have gone. Understanding what can be done with a simulation and how it can make one’s life as an artist easier, whilst at the same time exploding your animation potential, is one of the many superpowers of a 3D artist.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

In Blender, to create simple rigid body simulations in the Physics tab, add a Rigid Body set to Active for the object you wish to react to: wind or gravity.

If you want an object to be nothing but a reactive surface, set the Rigid Body to Passive. Then press Play to create the simulation

In Blender, to make an object a soft body, there are options, of which the Cloth modifier is the easiest to apply.

Make sure that any rigid bodies that you wish the cloth body to react to have the Collider modifier applied as well as the Rigid Body modifier. Again, press Play to create the simulation.

Fluid simulations are used to create water, and also fire and smoke. Usually these work differently to other simulations, in that a ‘volume’ needs to be created that marks the boundaries.

In Blender, even for fire, use the Fluid modifier in Physics to make objects part of these kinds of simulations

#9047. Miquel Navarro, Sculptor of Cities Real and Imagined, Dies at 81

In this column honoring those we lost in the art community, we remember a leading Spanish sculptor, a Dutch museum leader, and an Indian modernist.

In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world.

Miquel Navarro (1945–2026)Spanish sculptor of imaginary cities

The Spanish artist's hometown, Mislata in Valencia, served as a lifelong inspiration for his City sculptures, large-scale installations that invite visitors to walk through hundreds of abstract geometric shapes as skyscrapers. Fittingly enough, his imaginary cities became part of real urban landscapes, in the form of public works in Spain and abroad.

He was one of the artists to represent Spain at the 1986 Venice Biennale, and received the Spanish Ministry of Culture's Premio Nacional de Artes Plásticas (National Award for Plastic Arts) that same year. His work is in the collections of the Guggenheim museums in New York and Bilbao, Museo Reina Sofía, Centre Pompidou, and more.

"Today Mislata loses one of its most beloved residents, a friend and a genius," Mislata Mayor and President of Fundació Miquel Navarro Carlos Fernández Bielsa said in a statement translated from Spanish, "a generous person and a world-renowned figure in sculpture, an irreplaceable creator."

Ursula von Rydingsvard (1942–2026)Sculptor of monumental objects

Partially inspired by her childhood incarceration in post-World War II refugee camps, her enormous sculptures were whittled from massive cedar beams, including “Cedrus” (2016), an almost 20-foot-tall (~6 m) tornado made from 15,000 pounds (~6.8 t) of wood. Her work is in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and more.

“She was like the sun," Courtney Childress, her studio manager, said in this statement. "She was this force that pulled people in and kept them orbiting around her.”

#9046. Mamdani's Five Ballot Questions Pass, But Arts Groups Remain Skeptical

Concerns over landmark sites and lack of public input have dampened trust in Proposal 3, in particular.

Two arts organizations remain concerned that one of New York City's approved ballot measures could weaken review processes over public land usage, leaving areas such as landmark sites vulnerable to hasty sales and without sufficient community input.

All five ballot measures passed with strong support in yesterday's midterms, though the Municipal Art Society (MAS) of New York and the New York Landmarks Conservancy objected to parts of Proposal 3, which expedites the review of eligible projects in three areas: street safety construction, the sale or leasing of city-owned property, and the acquisition of office space for city employees.

Both groups, along with organizations such as the League of Women's Voters, have expressed varying levels of agreement with its three bundled target areas and called for them to be considered separately for independent review.

The measure is one of five put forth by the Commission on Government Efficiency, a 15-member panel assembled by Mayor Zohran Mamdani. All items aim to streamline city operations through revising the City Charter, such as reducing city contractor paperwork and setting aside a rainy-day fund in case of emergency.

"New York has had a strong tradition of public participation and robust debate, and over time, that's been chipped away," Andrea Goldwyn, the director of public policy at New York Landmarks Conservancy, told Hyperallergic.

Goldwyn's primary concern is with the second prong of Proposal 3, which reduces public review when the city sells or transfers unused development rights at landmark sites. Originally, most sales or leases of city-owned property underwent a seven-month review process called the Uniform Land Use Review Process (ULURP) and required City Council's final approval.

Proposal 3 allows projects not believed to have a sizeable impact on the surrounding environment to bypass final City Council approval and go through a 90-day fast lane called the Expedited Land Use Review Procedure (ELURP). Projects approved for ELURP can be concurrently reviewed by community boards and borough presidents, and city-owned landmarked property can be sold without City Council approval. Undevelopable land can additionally be sold to owners of adjacent properties without a public auction.

The proposal also excuses the Department of Transportation (DOT) from notifying elected officials and community boards before starting major projects deemed necessary for safety, and can instead notify those stakeholders when construction commences. Consultations with the Police Department, Fire Department, the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities, and the Department of Small Business Services remain mandatory.

"We've gotten calls from people who see new projects going up in their neighborhoods that they didn't know about," Goldwyn continued. "I think we're going to be seeing more of that because people aren't going to have the kind of notification they're used to having."

The final part of the proposal removes hearing requirements and approvals from the City Council and the City Planning Commission about acquiring or leasing office space for city employees, instead leaving it solely to Yume Kitasei, the commissioner for the Department of Citywide Administrative Services. Local community boards and all five borough presidents must still be notified of each proposal.

In an earlier statement, MAS stated that trimming down these review processes "could make it easier to sell or transfer valuable public land and development rights without sufficient safeguards to ensure lasting public benefits."

MAS called for a stronger framework that determines how public lands can be used. Such recommendations include prioritizing land for parks, affordable housing, and other projects that serve the public, rather than selling or leasing land to parties with unclear interests.

"Streamlining government processes should not come at the expense of public accountability or lasting community benefits," the statement adds.

The art team behind Order of the Sinking Star shares how Disney and Ghibli influenced the visuals and why a good-looking puzzle game must be clear first.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Order of the Sinking Star has more than 1,000 handcrafted puzzles spread across four distinct worlds, with a look that nods to classic Disney and Studio Ghibli. It launched on 8 October on PC, Nintendo Switch 2 and PS5. In my interview, indie game director Jonathan Blow (Braid, The Witness) and art lead Ethan Scheu explain how Thekla kept all that visual richness from getting in the way of the puzzles.

Blow’s brief was clear from the start, as he reveals the puzzle game “should be very easy to read the grid from the background, so it’s easy to tell where you can go, what is interactive and what is not, and so that your brain is never confused by what you are looking at.”

That idea shaped everything from character proportions to the technical features used to build the foreground play grids and how water is 'gridded' on each puzzle stage.

“One of my primary jobs in this department is just to look at a level and notice when my brain is working too hard,” Blow says. Sometimes the cause is a break with the grid, sometimes a background element that looks too “foregroundy”. There are general rules, but each level still needs its own judgement. The early days were rough, he says: “In the beginning we had a lot of problems here, but once we got the basic look of the game established, the art team was able to do many levels with relatively few problems.”

Scheu says artists have to unlearn some instincts: “As an artist, especially when starting on the project, your instincts and priorities for making something that might excite you are not necessarily aligned with making something clear and legible for the player.” Every artist on the project had to learn to picture a scene with clarity in mind. “We ultimately found that gameplay clarity and good visual design almost always go hand-in-hand, and getting this right became more second nature as the project progressed.”

The job continues after launch, as Scheu explains how, “Despite our effort to implement lessons we learned during development, issues and confusion as a result of artistic choices inevitably emerge once players start to interact with a finished level”.

Scheu explains how the art team takes notes from its game designers and player feedback, then works to remove ambiguity.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The levels come from several designers, so the art style had to work across some very different layouts. Blow sorts them into three types: “sometimes it’s a big open space with background behind it, sometimes it’s isles of varying shape (or cliffs similar to the isles), sometimes it’s tight irregular shapes that exactly determine where you can move.”

Get the style working across all three, and it can be applied to every level with fewer surprises, though Blow adds that making it look good “takes more work than it sounds when simply stated like that!”

Order of the Sinking Star also adapts earlier puzzle games, whose original looks were very different from the finished version. “We decided basically 100% of how they look […] we just had to decide harmoniously there,” Blow says.

Scheu says the team was “trying to achieve something very classic and illustrative, with a bit of a fairytale quality to it, without making it overly stylised or wildly proportioned.” Scenes were built “with a lot of depth, detail, atmosphere and rich surfaces, while keeping the gameplay areas easy to parse and devoid of distracting visual noise.”

He became art lead partway through development, when the characters, general settings and some stylistic choices were already established. His own aim was “to bring the fidelity and feeling of richness and timelessness closer to a level you might see from a large studio working with significant budgets, while figuring out ways to accomplish this with a very small team and limited resources.”

His influences came as much from outside games as from within them. “It’s nice to have a degree or two of separation of influence from the medium we work in,” he says. Also working on the game was concept artist Liz Pulido, whom he never got to work with directly, and whose work “has a very graceful and whimsical approach to design, form, and line-making that was a joy (and a challenge!) to try and portray.”

He also cites “Studio Ghibli’s approach to clean, vibrant stylised naturalism” as a huge inspiration. Watching classic Disney films with his young daughter had a similar effect. “I found myself awestruck by the rich attention to detail and whimsical quality of the backgrounds in films like Snow White and Sleeping Beauty, which until recently I had largely dismissed.”

The worlds share a set of visual rules, even though each has its own identity. “Despite the different worlds existing in their own unique settings, they were all crafted with the same guiding principles of style and construction, so there was never a lot of risk of the worlds clashing stylistically, at least,” Scheu says.

What separates them is geography and culture. “Creating the individual identities was more a matter of having the four worlds portray different biomes with distinct flora and geology, as well as distinct architectural, cultural, and geographic influences.”

That contrast does more than make each place look different. Each world has its own mechanics, characters, and stories, and the visual differences help give them distinct identities before the game brings them together. As those worlds collide and merge, their puzzle systems begin to intertwine, too.

With several designers contributing hundreds of levels, the art could easily drift. Scheu says, “We put significant effort into emphasising the play area and essential puzzle elements by achieving contrast in lighting, colour, value and scale.” The aim is “an immediate understanding of what is interactive, part of the grid, and relevant to the puzzle, while avoiding distraction from the background.”

Artists build levels from “a shared library of assets and materials and a modular approach to constructing levels”, which keeps the style consistent and the work moving. They also share work in progress with each other and the design team, and hold weekly feedback sessions to make sure everyone follows the same principles.

Differences are welcome, too. “We often choose to lean into the different approaches and stylistic instincts that individual artists take,” Scheu says. “Order of the Sinking Star is such an enormous game, we take advantage of the diversity of approach, style, and individual artistic preference simply to achieve more variety over hundreds of levels, as long as those core principles were maintained.”

“For most of development, the visuals were temporary,” Blow says. The engine was still being built, the features that make things look good weren’t there yet, and creative decisions “can only be provisional until all the final technology is in place”. The team only started trying to make the game look like the finished version “about the final 2-3 years of development”.

When Scheu joined, the vast majority of levels and the entire overworld still needed building. He took the chance to “do a bit of a reset in terms of how we were making assets and materials and constructing levels, not only to boost their quality level and fidelity, but to make the process more scalable and sustainable.”

Small teams can lean on individual strengths. “The magic of working on a small team like Thekla is that there is a real opportunity for individuals to bring certain skills or experience in techniques to the project that can have a huge impact,” Scheu says. Artist Jesse Seiterä, for example, “has significant experience and passion for creating lighting and atmosphere in scenes”, bringing techniques the project hadn’t had before.

The game runs on a custom engine built in Jai, the programming language Blow has been developing. For Scheu, the draw was that “we can tailor and streamline it to best serve the needs of our project, and avoid the bloat that comes with an engine built to serve many different types of applications.”

Because the engine grew alongside the game, a good idea could be turned into a feature quickly, “in some cases, the very same day, which was quite remarkable!” The result, he says, was an engine that “was very lean and fast and simple to use for our needs, which made it a real joy to work with as an artist.”

There’s a cost. “It inevitably takes longer for the feature set to reach maturity and start to feel really capable, and you might never have access to some of the more robust and flashy features you might see in an engine like Unreal.”

For Blow, the benefit is focus. “When you have a problem, you can really dial in on that problem and solve it effectively.” The atmospheric effects, he says, “are very closely tuned for the kinds of scenes we render, and would either be more expensive, or not look as good, in a generalised engine.”

Scheu is more cautious. “It’s hard to say if this is something that can’t be achieved in other engines, but what I can say is that we were really able to focus on and tailor effects for our specific needs.” The fog and clouds were used to create “a very specific effect and sense of depth and atmosphere”, and they help emphasise the play area in levels that would otherwise have vast and potentially distracting backgrounds.

On Jai, Blow’s praise is brief: “It compiles really fast, and it lets you do things very straightforwardly that are a pain in something like C++. And the metaprogramming is super powerful and useful.” Some language features were built and then dropped because “they ultimately didn’t add very much relative to the complexity of the implementation”. Relative pointers and automated SOA struct generation are two examples. Starting again, he’d cut that experimentation, “but of course when you can’t see the future, this kind of experimentation is necessary!”

Thekla plans to release the engine as open source. “This is meant to be a lean-meat, low-fat engine,” Blow says. “We want to provide an example of a commercial-quality shipping game, in open source, so that people can build from a good starting point.”

He adds a warning: “It’s not a no-programmer-involved engine like Unreal or Unity can be […] you’d still need a good programmer to get a good result here.”

Scheu says, “I don’t think I can speak to this with much knowledge,” but expects that “any team using it would need to heavily modify and develop it for the needs of their own project.”

All this work went into creating Order of the Sinking Star, a puzzle game that promises over 500 hours of gameplay for the most dedicated puzzle solvers across more than 1,000 interconnected puzzles. It's the kind of easy-to-play but complex-to-complete puzzle game Jonathan Blow has been renowned for since Braid, and especially since the Myst-like The Witness.

Part of that accessibility comes from Order of the Sinking Star also letting you find your own way through its enormous world. Each of the game's four realms has its own mechanics and characteristics, and if you hit a wall in one, you can head elsewhere and return later. As the worlds begin to merge, the puzzles start borrowing from one another, opening up new combinations of ideas.

Order of the Sinking Star is available now on PC (Steam and Steam Deck), Nintendo Switch 2 and PlayStation 5.

#9044. France Opens War Crimes Investigation Into Israeli Airstrike That Killed Artist Ali Cherri's Parents

Amnesty International found that Israeli forces had no evidence of a verifiable military target at the site of the strike.

France's War Crimes Unit has opened an investigation into a deadly Israeli airstrike on French-Lebanese artist and filmmaker Ali Cherri's family home in Barbour, Beirut. The investigation emerges seven months after the artist filed a complaint accusing Israel of war crimes with the office, as the 2024 strike on the residential building killed both of his parents, the domestic worker they employed in the apartment Cherri owned, and at least four other civilians living in the building.

In a February report on Israeli war crimes in Lebanon, Amnesty International stated that Israeli forces had no evidence of a verifiable military target at the site of the strike, and concluded that Israeli forces failed to issue an evacuation warning to civilians before conducting the strike on the 12-story apartment building on November 26, 2024 — less than 12 hours before the temporary ceasefire between Hezbollah and Israel came into effect. Constructed by the Cherri family, the building suffered structural damage localized to the eastern apartments on the 7th to 10th floors. Cherri's late parents, Mahmoud Naim Cherri and Nadira Hayek, as well as domestic worker Birki Negesa, were found in the wreck of the artist's ninth-floor apartment where they resided.

Cherri and his legal representatives at the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) also commissioned the London-based investigative research agency Forensic Architecture to digitally reconstruct the apartment building based on the artist's and neighboring witnesses' documentation of the site post-strike. Both Amnesty International's and Forensic Architecture's findings informed Cherri's complaint accusing Israel of war crimes by “intentionally directing an attack against a civilian object.”

#9043. New York Studio School revamp unearths long-forgotten murals

Back in 1907, Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney established her sculpture studio in a converted stable and hayloft on MacDougal Alley in the heart of Manhattan’s Greenwich Village. The heiress and artist then proceeded to procure four neighbouring brownstones one by one, with the Lincoln Memorial sculptor Daniel Chester French being the last holdout.

The five buildings that now comprise 8 West 8th Street are some of the New York art world’s most storied. It was here that Whitney promoted US artists at a time when they were widely denigrated, and where she opened the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1931. After the museum relocated uptown, the nascent New York Studio School (NYSS) moved into the compound in 1967.

Over the past century Edward Hopper sketched, John Cage lectured and Philip Guston taught within these walls. Countless other greats practised, exhibited or, in the case of Marianne Faithfull, lived in what is now a National Historic Landmark. “This building has been the incubator for American art for 120 years,” says the artist Matthew Ritchie, sitting in a bare-bones conference room on a warm September afternoon. It has also been sorely in need of a makeover at least since he was a student here in the 1990s.

When Ritchie was named the school’s director last year, the roof and studio skylights—coveted by students for their diffused natural light—leaked, the nearly century-old cloth-wrapped wiring had deteriorated dangerously and wheelchair access was extremely limited. His priority was renovation. The first phase—including doubling the public exhibition space and creating a new accessible lecture and performance hall in wood with stepped seating—is set to be completed this autumn, and phase two will begin in the spring.

Prior to Ritchie’s arrival, the school had obtained public grants for the necessary work, but they required matching funds and their expiration date was fast approaching. He quickly marshalled forces. The board agreed to donate the required money, he says, and the school tapped Matthew Baird of Baird Architects to helm the overhaul.

The renovation work uncovered an early work by the British-born artist Cecily Brown painted on the wall when she was a student there in the 1990s

Ritchie and Baird’s history of collaboration dates back 17 years and across two other local institutions. In 2009, they teamed up to consider the effects of rising sea levels on the built environment as part of the interdisciplinary Rising Currents project at the Museum of Modern Art. Just a few years later, they put their theories into practice after Hurricane Sandy tore through the city, its storm surge flooding much of downtown. Ritchie was on the board of the beloved alternative art space The Kitchen when it enlisted Baird to rehabilitate its waterlogged lobby and black-box theatre.

The architect’s sensitive execution on that project—he preserved visual evidence of flood damage, for example—made him an obvious choice for the NYSS project, which presented a similar challenge. “You have this really cool building that’s got this patina of great artists that have moved through it,” Baird says. “How do you not erase that?”

Thanks to Baird and Ritchie’s handle-with-care edict, the construction crew was on the lookout for treasures buried beneath layers of plasterboard. The artist Cecily Brown had told Ritchie that she painted her first mural on a school wall when she was a student in the 1990s but could not remember where. And the school archives held numerous photos of murals Whitney had commissioned from the artist Robert E. Locher for the original carriage house.

Sure enough, the crew uncovered the work of both artists within a 24-hour period. Brown’s piece—featuring disembodied penises, two of them appearing to kiss—is in the newly expanded gallery space on the main floor. To prevent it from potentially distracting from exhibitions, the design team installed a shallow cabinet in front of the mural.

Ritchie jokes that the set-up resembles a gabinetto segreto, or secret room, the most famous of which was a locked vault of erotic artefacts from Pompeii and Herculaneum. “Who doesn’t want a Cecily Brown mural? And then, who doesn’t want pornography in your brand-new public gallery?” he says with a laugh. “It’s the perfect combination.”

A recently uncovered mural by the artist Robert E. Locher, commissioned by Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney

Workers discovered the two Locher murals where a bathroom and a hallway leading to it will be built. Intended to be viewed in the candlelight of Whitney’s dining room, one is a glimmering green, the other a trompe l’oeil image of doric columns. Baird tweaked the layout but not the location of the restroom. “Now it will be the most historic bathroom in New York,” Ritchie says.

A less fortuitous surprise: the beams beneath Robert Winthrop Chanler’s flame-motif fireplace in Whitney’s original second-floor studio were cracking, requiring emergency shoring up to stop the ceiling from collapse—together with the priceless fireplace. “This is the urgency of renovation,” Ritchie says. “You can wait too long, and then you lose it all.”

Because of the grant deadlines for the first phase of the project, Baird needed to work at warp speed, condensing three years of planning, permitting, bidding and execution into one. Owing to New York City’s complex building code, he approached the $2.2m renovation as “100 small projects” rather than gutting the 59,000 sq. ft building. The landmark-restoration specialist Jonathan Raible is overseeing the new roof.

In addition to enhancing the first floor’s public spaces, Baird rewired the building, renovated the wreck of a kitchen and improved accessibility by adding a wheelchair lift to the performance hall. “You can’t have a public programme if you don’t provide correct facilities for the public,” Ritchie says. “You’re not really welcoming them.”

Climbing the narrow staircases to the maze of studios where the school’s 27 full-time, in-person students work, Baird speaks enthusiastically about the second phase of renovations, which will include a student coffee bar. In keeping with his preservationist instincts, he plans to relamp with LED bulbs the elegant Fresnel recessed box lighting that Whitney installed for evenly washed walls, and he hopes to restore the system of baffles that modulated direct light in the studios as well as undertake other restoration while safeguarding the landmark’s character.

Ritchie already has his eye on another, likely longer-term fix for the school: free tuition. “That would require a very large endowment from extremely generous single or multiple donors,” he says, giving his best impression of a silver-tongued salesman, “which we’re eagerly awaiting with an entirely unique naming opportunity.”

#9041. The Prior Occupants of Westbeth Are Just Beyond Reach

A little more legibility would've benefited Alison Nguyen's fragmented short film about the famed NYC artists' housing complex.

Near the start of the High Line in Manhattan, a short film screening to the public above 14th Street dances around the history of the Westbeth Artists Housing complex, a stone's throw away from the park. While clearly drawn from extensive research and intrigue, Alison Nguyen's 14-minute film “Prior Occupants” (2026) skates on vague fragments of information that do better to incite curiosity rather than illustrate outright.

Have you ever sat through a lecture while feverishly looking up the keywords being mentioned to appear less woefully out of the loop? Nguyen begins by paging through confidential files attributed to the American industrial development company Bell Laboratories, but does little to explain their significance beyond fleeting references to the company's involvement in the Manhattan Project and developing components for ballistic missiles.

It's the best use of negative space since the FedEx logo.

When it comes to clever logo designs, nothing beats a bit of negative space. From the NBC Peacock to perhaps the most famous example, the FedEx arrow, blank space can give an otherwise simple design an ingenious double meaning. And here's a brilliantly simple example that's sending sparks through Reddit.

"I've come across this logo from time to time and I'm so jealous I did not think of it. So simple and I love negative space," a Redditor comments alongside a logo for a brand called Ed's Electric. While it looks like it simply depicts a plug and a socket, take a look at that white space and you'll spoon spot an 'E' for 'Ed'. Like all of the best logos, this one is guaranteed to make you double-take.

"Negative space really is something; if you see the hidden wordmark, you can no longer unsee it," one user comments, while another adds, "That is top level design!"

The Ed's Electric logo was designed for a local company by Josiah Jost many years ago. Based in Canada, Jost has worked with clients from 55+ countries. Commenting on a Facebook post featuring the design earlier this year, Jost said, "I designed Ed’s Electric back in 2008 - glad to see it still getting coverage."
