Not only does the design make it look like the phrase says 'Anal Malaysia', it also looks like there's a figure squatting down between the two words. Quite how this made it through rounds of approval we're not sure. It leaves us asking whether anyone gave it a look over other than the original designer.

But the potential pitfalls of typography go further than the example above. It's sometimes not enough to only check that your design reads well on a horizontal plane. It's best to check how it looks when turned in other directions too.

The UK Office of Government Commerce existed from 2000 to 2011 with the objective of improving efficiency in public spending. In 2007 it commissioned FHD to design a new logo that would show the body's bold commitment to driving up standards. The problem was that the logo was printed on pens, mouse mats, and all manner of other stationery items that would be viewed from different orientations.

It took the government department's employees mere seconds to notice something that the logo's designers hadn't. Rotated 90 degrees the logo looks rather rude. Incredibly, the OGC decided to stick with the new logo. A spokesperson even quipped: "It is not inappropriate to an organisation that's looking to have a firm grip on Government spend."

Oh my! These days, there’s a graphics department out there that might not have meant to get its lighting decoration go viral... The fact is that #kerning/spacing isn't just a #designer's nitpick! Enjoy a little giggle with this one 🤪🤣 #DesignFail #MarketingFail pic.twitter.com/Uf4qqGG9m8December 6, 2019

Choosing the right font is only the start when it comes to ensuring the typography is right for a design, and that applies to packaging as well as anything else. A little kerning to add space between the 'L' and the 'I' would have been a good idea to prevent misreadings of the product name in the case above.

Always run your design by several people and ask them what they see. Chances are they might have a very different interpretation from those who know what the message is intended to be. And tread very carefully when the word you're designing has any similarity at all to a word you want to avoid.

"As he watches, her body drifts below the water's surface, forever altered. Before he disposes of each victim, he takes a trophy. It's a sign of his power, and a warning…" We're not sure that this novel sounds like the best read out there, but we would never go so far as to demand this fate for the author.

There are many ways to establish text hierarchy – through font, weight, colour, location of text – and sometimes tweaking more than one of these is necessary. In this case, switching from all caps to title case was not enough to prevent an unintended reading of this design, with title placed directly under the author's name. Remember that as a designer, you're not only responsible for how things look but also for their context and how they'll be read.

Perhaps one of the most notorious packaging blunders in history came from this own-brand buttermilk sold by Tesco in Ireland. This shot with crease in the right place went viral and was even picked up by several newspapers after it was taken at a supermarket in Dublin.

Shopper Andy Burdens wrote on Reddit at the time: "They really made a cock and balls of this branding." Tesco changed the design after the media coverage of the blunder. The lesson here? No design is too small or routine to merit making a mockup – designer Oisín Hurst told Creative Bloq he designed the piece on a flat keyline and didn't mock it up, thinking, "it was buttermilk – what could go wrong?"

Logos often combine ideas taken from a brand's name or function. It makes sense then that this bakery in Greece would consider combining a representation of the eponymous 'mama' and the oven in which she presumably bakes her exquisite cakes and breads. The problem is that the position of the flame in the oven makes it look like something else.

It's hard to imagine the designers weren't aware of how it looked and the design may have paid off, the bakery and cafe still proudly using the logo that has taken it to international internet fame.

In general, designers need to be careful with employing the human figure in logos as so many decisions can be misinterpreted, as is demonstrated very well by this 1970s logo for the Catholic Church Archdiocesan Youth Commission. We can perhaps ascribe it to more naive times. And after all, designers can't be expected to predict all future associations that will emerge related to their clients.

The design of marketing campaigns has grown now to encompass a lot more than graphic design. Campaigns often now also include elements of UI and the whole user experience involved in what more interactive initiatives aimed at promoting customer engagement. This kind of marketing has to be well thought through though.

Coca-Cola's custom bottle creator campaign for Pride Month resulted in embarrassment for the company when it turned out the programme would reject certain words from inclusion in the bottles, as well as swear words, the list of banned words seemed to include LGBT, transgender, black lives matter (but not white lives matter) and Palestine.

Presented without comment. cc Venn Diagram enthusiast @LadyFOHF pic.twitter.com/RjYAUjlJaVAugust 14, 2014

This one was a bit of a clanger for the media conglomerate Thomson Reuters. The idea was presumably to suggest that the concepts on the left are the group's core values, but the image looks like a Venn diagram, a type of diagram used to show logical relations between different sets through overlapping curves. Read this way, the graphic appears to show that there is very little overlap between the values on the left and the comparably minute values of Thomson Reuters.

The Washington Post even picked up on the slip and praised the company for its honesty in the ironic headline, "In refreshing change of pace, company admits it's not innovative." The lesson here is to always step back and consider whether design elements you have chosen for purely aesthetic purposes may resemble any other visual language in common use.

Well-heeled travellers will have been a little taken aback when they saw this edition of Where Milan, which is published by Proedi and distributed at many of the city's most exclusive hotels. Placement of the photo cutout layered over the title makes it seem that the publishers are calling into question the reputation of their own cover model.

It's an Italian publication, so the designers could perhaps be forgiven for overlooking an error when working in a foreign language, but if you're aiming at a foreign language market, you need to be able to spot a howler like this.

Another packaging delight, this nutritional supplement from CVS appears to be marketed for Hannibal Lecter. The problem here stems from making assumptions about what the customer knows and following the format of other items in a range of products rather than adapting the design.

For other supplements in this range at US pharmacy chain there's no confusion. The text can read Chewable Vitamin C and no unintentionally comic meaning arises, but with this product it may have been better to clarify in an appropriately sized type that the products inside are tablets avoid skin-crawling misinterpretations.

This is apparently an advert for a graduation day photography service. Getting on the career track maybe? The light at the end of the tract representing a new dawn? Whatever the original intention, there's no getting over the fact that this graduate does not come across as overjoyed about her prospects on the modern job market. In fact, it looks like she's about to end it all by walking straight into an oncoming train.

The colour tones and even the choice of font seem to only back up the impression that the intended message is more about bereavement than celebrating graduation, with the light of the oncoming train perhaps also representing some hope that there may be some better world in the next life. Always consider the mood you want to convey and ensure colours, imagery and type are on message.

It's vital to remember that design is ultimately about clear communication. Just as a writer or speaker needs to choose the perfect words to deliver their message, designers must communicate theirs by selecting the correct visual elements, which convey exactly what they want to say.

Graphic designers producing promotional material and visuals for technical instructions can benefit from having a clear understanding themselves of how the product they're depicting actually works.

When it comes to technology, if the visual material produced for the product doesn't get it right, what chance do the digital immigrants among the customer base have? Just as an aside, we love how retro this design for selfie stick packaging already looks.

These cycling shorts let you fart while riding a bike. It's a neat feature, right? But really who decided it was a good idea to communicate the breathability of these padded shorts by overlaying some gas emerging from the padded rear end?

Sometimes designers have to accept that no designing is needed at all and that conveying a message can be better accomplished by the accompanying text, with no need for added visual clarification.

Looks like I picked a bad day to set this app up pic.twitter.com/R11M7RNU86December 12, 2019

A little UI blooper to finish with. We're not sure why different parts of the world adopted different standard formats for expressing something as straightforward as the date and it is a phenomenon that causes problems for designers everywhere working on UI forms, but this is something that the designer should have foreseen. When you're working with dates or with any other variable content think through all of the possible scenarios that could arise.

He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

#9002. Andrea Bowers Salutes the Climate Change Activists of the 1980s at Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo

Andrea Bowers’ solo exhibition “La Ragnatela” at the Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo in Turin, Italy, is unintentionally, aptly timed, given its focus on the politics of climate change: Last year, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni hit pause on solar panels on farmland, calling it a “threat to our food sovereignty.”

Bowers’ show spotlights the Italian anti-nuclear feminist movement and women’s camp La Ragnatela—“the spiderweb”, in Italian—that launched in 1983 in Comiso, Sicily, to protest the installation of US nuclear cruise missiles at the NATO base in Comiso. The show is a mini-retrospective composed of Bowers’ political activist work which was in dialogue with the movement. There are works by Bowers that she created in 2003, straight out of graduate school, as well as pieces produced in 2013, 2022, 2023 and four newly created artworks for the exhibition. Related Articles Melting Ron DeSantis Statue Makes a Point About Climate Change in Florida Collective Climate Action Implemented by Los Angeles Arts Institutions

Much of La Ragnatela’s history has been forgotten, so Bowers worked with curator Bernardo Follini to find and rebuild the network of Italian ecofeminists. Follini found three women, who are now in their 80s and 90s, who contributed documents and clippings to the exhibition.

“The social engagement part of my practice is the least known about or documented because the art world is more focused on objects, but this is what I’m most proud of,” said Bowers during a preview in Turin, dressed in head-to-toe black with her Botticelli-esque hair flowing freely.

The show opens with Defense of Necessity (2003), a quilt that nods to women’s traditional crafts, and it’s one of the first pieces that Bowers created as a political artist. On close inspection of the quilt, there are sowings of spiderwebs, a symbol for the Women’s Pentagon Action, an American grassroots ecofeminist and anti-nuclear movement that was simultaneously taking place in Italy by way of La Ragnatela and in England with the Greenham Common Women’s Peace Encampment. Defense of Necessity is held up as a fence in the show. “The fence is the site often where nonviolence is questioned whether it’s becoming violence. Activists who are involved in nonviolence are always saying, if we cut that fence, does it become violence? Or is this called an offense of necessity, which is an argument that smaller injustices, or you break small laws to protect the world from larger injustices,” explained Bowers. “It’s a legal term and because it has the word ‘fence’ in it, it’s a play on words and it’s poetic.”

On the other side of the fence are four vitrine cases, two of which feature a timeline of the La Ragnatela movement. The others display letter exchanges between the women in Comiso and their comrades in England, who eventually traveled to Comiso to help them protest. There are photographs of some of the women who were arrested for protesting, along with a letter from one of the women, who was detained for a long time and put on trial, during which she wore a T-shirt that says “question authority.” Bowers took the tagline and added it to Neon Spiderweb #3 (2026), a neon spiderweb with the words sitting on the outer string of a web—the artist also made three other neon works with such slogans: “A better end of the world is possible,” “Return our future” and “To be free from fear.” The political slogans of hope pour over into Political Ribbons (2026), brightly colored sheets of silky ribbons that repeat the mottos on the neon signs or feature new sayings: “People over profits,” “Outlaw women are the only hope for earth’s survival” and “Widen the web to break the nuclear chain.” Visitors are urged to take ribbons from the wall with them when they visit the show. Bowers explains that it’s a “simple way for people to take a position.” It’s a methodology that she’s used before, adding that to this day, she still gets a thrill out of seeing them in the wild or online.

Bowers’ pieces in the show command attention no matter their size. Her graphite on paper works: Diabloblockade, Diablo Nuclear Power Plant, Abalone Alliance, 198 (2003) and Women’s Pentagon Action, 1981, Detail of Woven Web Around Pentagon (2003) are hyperrealistic. the artist has recreated photographs that were given to her by her mother’s friends who were part of the Californian eco-group Mother for Peace. In Cardboard (2026), a larger-than-life cardboard with an “empowered Italian woman” facing her back to the audience holding a flag that says “Sun and wind,” the artist taught herself how to use an iPad to draw the image that’s been projected onto a thick cardboard.

The show at the Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo is sort of a homecoming for Bowers, as she last showed at the foundation in 1998 as part of a group show titled “Guarene 98.” Some 28 years later, her pieces from the Chandeliers of Interconnectedness franchise grace the halls of the space as visitors make their way to other exhibitions by Nan Goldin or Joseph Yaeger. The show, however, feels cut short. Perhaps Bowers has more to say than can fit the space she was given. (It would have been a better idea to give her two galleries to really demonstrate two decades of hard passion for the environment.)

Still, she managed to make a mark with Neon Opland (2026), another neon sign that imitates a doodle from a La Ragnatela poster of a woman kicking a missile with the words “No ai missile” written beneath. It’s somewhat phallic, a comical touch made more apparent by teenage couple who were flirting on a bench opposite its neon lights.

#9001. Atelier Zébulon Perron draws on metabolist influence for Montreal bistro

A monochrome palette and influences from Japanese metabolism characterise Bistrot à Franky in Montreal, Canada designed by local outfit Atelier Zébulon Perron.

The restaurant is a home base for local chef Francis Blais in the city’s hip Mile End neighbourhood.

Atelier Zébulon Perron took what it views as the standard design language of a Montreal bistro – bright lighting and lots of activity – and translated it into a more contemporary design.

For studio founder Zebulon Perron, the monochrome whites and beiges, interspersed with milled aluminium accents and a large zinc bar top, allowed the studio to experiment with textures and lighting to create visual interest and contrast in the dining space.

“With the monochromy of the restaurant, we experimented with textures – shiny versus matte, tile nd and stucco – and how light reacts to those surfaces in different ways,” Perron told Dezeen.

The studio emphasised the postmodern and “retrofuturist” elements of the design, pointing to the custom chandeliers with their illuminated Pyrex tubes and exposed wiring, fabricated by Perron’s long-time collaborators, local lighting design studio Lambert & Fils.

Perron highlighted the milled aluminium wine cellar that sits above the bar face, interspersed with portholes that are a direct reference to Japanese metabolist architecture.

“There’s a postmodern, 1980s aesthetic that naturally rose from everything we were doing,” said Perron.

Visitors enter the restaurant through a red-painted hallway and a metal door and handle carved from butcher block by local cabinetmaker Olivier Doray.

Inside, only the terrazzo floor was a holdover from the building’s former use. Granite tabletops cover some of the larger tables, while the classic bistrot white tablecloths are draped over the smaller tables.

Blond leather banquettes were placed below large mirrors on the wall opposite the bar, and these larger seating arrangements are centred by large butcher block tables, also fabricated by Doray.

Custom walnut chairs were designed by local industrial designer Guillaume Sasseville.

On the walls, white tile is interspersed with stucco and works of art, curated by local filmmaker Xavier Dolan. These artworks give pops of colour and Perron said that the monochromatic design elements allow both the food and the artworks to stand out in the space.

“Since the canvas is pretty neutral, the food and the artwork take centre stage,” he said.

A set of windows opens up the kitchen space to the dining room.

Custom bar seating features white columns with seats informed by transportation design, and Perron noted that the metal details and clean lines of the bar space, as well as the metal fans, also give the interior a streamlined look.

Atelier Zébulon Perron has designed some of the most interesting interior spaces in the city, including Café Constance and the dining areas for the city’s Four Seasons hotel.

It also helped create the pop-up bar staged during the city’s inaugural design week earlier this year.

The issue of AI-generated music on Spotify is causing controversy again, but this time with a twist. While the streaming service says it's cracking down on AI slop, it's also planning to let users generate their own AI remixes and covers (and to charge them for it).

The pricing and timeframe is not yet fully defined, but, according to the Financial times, Spotify aims to launch AI remixing by around February 2027 for a $4-$5 monthly surcharge on top of the price of a standard Premium plan. So far the reaction among both users and musicians has been tepid, but visual artists should also be watching what happens.

Spotify's proposal might seem reasonable. AI remixing will be an optional feature for users who want it, and artists can choose whether to opt in to license their work for it. For those who do, their fans get new ways to engage with their music, and they receive a new stream of royalties.

That sounds reassuring until you consider how platforms like Spotify work. If enough artists join, participation could quickly turn into an economic necessity. If remixable songs receive more engagement, appear in more playlists and generate more activity, non-remixable work could become harder to discover. There's also a concern that AI-generated remixes themselves could crowd out original music.

Beyond Spotify, It's also a test case for a question facing every creative sector. Should technology help audiences discover artistic work, or treat art as raw material for endless algorithmic recombination?

In Spotify's vision, a listener might turn a ballad into a dance track or make one artist appear to perform another artist's song. The value shifts from the original work to how much it’s ‘reimagined’.

On social media, TikTok and Instagram already allow users’ visual content to be ‘remixed’. Applying the same concept to art transforms it from something we experience into something we personalise. Think the artist chose the wrong pitch? Change it. Don’t like the ending of a movie? Generate a different one

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

On Spotify’s own community forum, one person describes this as like spitting in the face of artists. It trivialises their intent and judgment.

Art's power often comes from the fact that someone else made the decisions. The point of encountering another person's creativity is not that it reflects our own preferences, but that it shows us a perspective we didn't have before. When every creative decision becomes are our own choice, artistic intent becomes insignificant . That's bad not just for the artists, it also for the consumer's ability to critique art.

#8999. Ten products that upgrade office interiors

The following products for offices published on our Showroom section allow for streamlined workplaces that don’t compromise on aesthetics.

These include desks, sit-stand tables as well as those with integrated outlets, modular seating systems and ergonomic task chairs.

Global designers and brands aimed to boost productivity through these items, whether that be by reducing desktop clutter, providing spontaneous opportunities for meetings and light work, or correcting posture to make long periods of sitting less taxing on the body.

Read on to find out more about this selection of workplace furniture.

TOT table by Isern Serra for Omelette Editions

A bisected tabletop with electrical outlets tucked neatly inside characterises this co-working desk by Spanish designer Isern Serra for furniture brand Omelette Editions

Supported by cylindrical legs, the TOT table provides a 12-socket power board, allowing wires to be neatly concealed to eliminate excess visual and physical tabletop clutter.

Muku task chair by Foster + Partners for Okamura

Japanese furniture brand Okamura has released a sleek office chair designed by eminent British studio Foster + Partners.

Muku comes in a sober trio of colourways – light grey, dark grey, red and black – all partly made from recycled materials: recycled aluminium for the frames, and recycled fishing nets for the mesh seat upholstery.

Pullman Modular seating system by NaughtOne

All three segments in the Pullman Modular system feature high backs, creating visual seclusion, sound-dampening and room division in open plan interiors.

Dynamism is given to steel and plywood in this task chair by designer Alina Schnizler for German brand Wilkhahn.

WiChair features a thick, strong spring beneath its seat, which gives bounce to the structure and encourages active sitting.

Indoor landscapes are created via this undulating modular sofa system created by designer Francesco Rota and Italian brand Lapalma.

HUB aims to create islands of activity in open plan spaces, creating space for working, meeting, conversing and waiting.

TNK500 Aurea task chair by Alegre Design for Actiu

Spanish brand Actiu worked with design firm Alegre Design on this task chair, which has a distinctively metallically-finished frame.

TNK500 Aurea supports healthy posture when working, and is made from almost 60 per cent recycled materials.

Konzert office furniture system by Paolo Dell’Elce for Knoll

Complete private office fit-outs are made cohesive with US furniture brand Knoll and Italian designer Paolo Dell’Elce’s new furnishing system.

Konzert comprises configurable wall panels, tables, seating and storage that come in various curated colourways and finishes.

Seated and standing work and meetings alike are made possible by this series of tables by office furniture brand Actiu.

Menssula sit-stand work tables come in various sizes and formats, all containing an electrically-powered height raising mechanism.

Norwegian designers Andreas Engesvik and Jannicke Grung have created a compact and lighthearted task chair for Flokk-owned furniture brand HÅG

HÅG Minu comes in seven designer-curated curated colourways and aims to bring the comfort and casualness of residential furniture to workplaces.

British furniture brand Boss Design aimed to bring adaptability and personalisation to this range of office booths.

Eden pods can be fitted out with lounge furniture, tactile cladding and finishes, and planters on their roofs to bring the health and wellbeing of plants into workplaces.

#8998. After a Democratic Victory in Midterm Elections, Trump Focuses on Touting His Ballroom: ‘This Is a Special Structure’

After a midterm election that saw the Democrats take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate on Tuesday night, President Donald Trump spent Wednesday ignoring the results and instead stumping for his $400 million plan to build a ballroom for the White House.

Trump’s ballroom has been controversial from the start, not only because he demolished the White House’s East Wing to make room for it but also because he said it would include a military complex beneath the structure. A series of challenges, both from past presidents and US courts, have questioned whether Trump even has the authority to undertake such a project. And yet, he has largely stuck to his guns, once even labeling the ballroom “THE GREATEST OF ITS KIND!” Related Articles In Fiery Court Filing, Democratic Lawmaker Says Kennedy Center's Closure Is Meant to Hide Its Failure Under Trump Former Presidents Obama, Clinton Mock Trump's White House Interiors With Comparisons to 'Saddam Hussein' and 'Liberace's Bathroom'

Whether Trump would be able to fully proceed with the ballroom plan under a Democratic-majority House and Senate remains an open question. The ballroom has been the subject of a lawsuit brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which aimed to halt its construction. In September, the Supreme Court ruled that it could go forward, saying the National Trust didn’t have the legal grounds to bring the suit.

But Trump seemed totally unbothered Wednesday as he spoke during a ceremony intended to mark the raising of the final beam on the structure. “This is a special structure,” he said, according to the New York Times. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world.”

Regarding his repeated efforts to add to or amend preexisting structures in Washington, D.C., he said, “You know, it was sort of mentioned a little bit during the campaign: ‘Why does Trump spend time on the White House?’ Well, first of all, it’s very little time. Second of all, I like it. It’s good. For me, it’s relaxing.”

#8997. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

#8996. Dubai Design Week's 12th edition celebrates bold Middle Eastern design

From an eye-catching exhibition spotlighting geometric forms to installations designed by prominent architects, Dubai Design Week is set to host its 12th edition to honour the Middle East’s vibrant design, craft and culture.

The programme takes place across Dubai Design District (d3), the city’s creative hub, from 3 to 8 November 2026.

The festival’s headline event is Downtown Design, an annual fair that spotlights regional and global design brands, makers and manufacturers.

Dezeen readers can get 50 per cent off their tickets using the code DESIGN50.

Taking place from 4 to 8 November,  Downtown Design presents site-specific installations, talks and networking series and exhibitions for furniture, textiles, lighting and kitchen and bathroom products.

This year, British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has added his creative touch to Veuve Clicquot‘s annual lounge at the fair, which will serve as a place to relax, as well as a venue to host talks and parties.

Italian design brand Memphis Milano will also unveil an exhibition that honours the bright colours and geometric forms utilised by the group’s founder Ettore Sottsass in the 1980s, known as the Memphis movement.

Also returning to the 2026 edition is the UAE Designer Exhibition – a platform for emerging talent in the emirate within a B2B and B2C environment, creating a space for future mentorship.

Under the theme Inherited Futures, the exhibition features 30 UAE-based designers’ works, which will focus on materiality, form and technology.

With architect AlZaina Lootah as design collaborator, the exhibition tasks contributors to design products that are producible, durable, high-quality and referential to cultural contexts.

Alongside the fair, Dubai Design Week will also exhibit installations across the district, created by global architecture practices Nikken Sekkei, Sobokuya, Aestudio, Alter, Palm and Palazzo, design firm Dubai Duette Studio, architect Rasha Saffarini, cultural platform Avid Learning Middle East and craft group Dakhnii Diaries.

Programme highlights also include the annual Urban Commission competition, which will showcase the winning proposal by Dubai-based studio Nao Architects.

Titled Three Gardens and a Room, Nao Architects’ installation responds to the competition’s theme Atmospheres, which asked participants to consider “how light, temperature, sound, material and spatial design shape how we feel, move and connect”.

On display for the duration of the design week, the installation by the practice’s founder Reem Nassour reconsiders a garden with four key architectural elements – a roof, mound, hearth and enclosure – in the form of three gardens connected by a central room.

Abwab, Dubai Design Week’s flagship commissioning programme, presents In Other Words, a group exhibition open from 3 to 8 November.

The exhibition presents commissioned works by five selected practices from West, South, Southeast and East Asia, and Africa.

Its overarching theme explores communication beyond speech and writing, addressing symbols and gestures used throughout history.

Other exhibitions curated for the 2026 edition include the Worlds Ahead: 25 Years of Design, Place and Impact in the Middle East exhibition by architecture studio Woods Bagot, and the showcase by Paris’ L’école School of Jewellery Arts, which is supported by jewellery brand Van Cleef and Arpels.

Dubai Design Week’s Marketplace also returns for the latest iteration from 7 to 8 November, serving as a platform for independent makers across the Middle East.

The platform enables artisans to sell their handmade pieces, from fashion and jewellery to homeware and food, and offers a series of live performances and culinary experiences.

The festival is held under the patronage of Her Highness Sheikha Latifa bint Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, chairperson of the Dubai Culture and Arts Authority (Dubai Culture).

Last year, it seemed that some of the biggest brands had declared the death of the opulent, magical holiday advert. AI slop would do, they decided.

Coca-Cola's AI Christmas ad was one of the most controversial, while McDonald's pulled its festive effort due to the backlash. This year, it seems we're seeing a strong counter movement, with big brands making a point of their commitment to handcrafted art.

First, there was the glorious Prada Christmas ad, directed by former Disney animator John Pomeroy. Now Levi's has pulled out the stops for a very different animated gem, showing that it's not just luxury brands that see the value of human craftsmanship in advertising.

Levi's Let’s Get Fuzzy stop-motion holiday campaign was produced by the London-based production studio Blinkink . The animation begins as a play on horror movies, making it a fun segue from Halloween. A monster interrupts a group of friends' cosy festive retreat in a snow-covered cabin. But Fuzzyeti's discovery of festive jumpers makes him quickly succumb to the holiday spirit.

The medium of painstaking stop-motion animation was chosen to highlight Levi's heritage of craftsmanship. As shown in the making of video below, a six-person team spent more than 2,000 hours over six and a half weeks building and painting the sets, including three cabins at different scales, along with 400 miniature trees, and four faces for each character.

The clothes are miniature replicas of real Levi's products – a stylist was on hand to ensure accuracy. They were moved for every frame of the animation to make them feel life like, but requiring four hours of work of every second of animation.

A reference edit was made with actors and the directors themselves acting out the roles (including a specialist monster actor for Fuzzyyeti). This was then used as the guide for the animators.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Levi's has form in animation, from the psychedelic 2D short The Stranger in 1971 to Clayman with Shaggy’s Boombastic in claymation in 1995. Today, the decision to use such a laborious handcrafted process makes a bigger statement, creating added distinction and value amid so much AI-generated content.

Your local food truck might not worry about their ugly AI flyers if they can do the job for cheap. But for big brands, proof of work like the behind-the-scenes video above has become as important as the finished advert. Avoiding the embarrassment of an 'AI content' label isn't enough, they're taking steps to proactively signal that an advert was human made.

Hermès and Ralph Lauren are just two fashion brands that have been doing this by mentioning the people behind their ads in the captions on social media. Naming the creative team behind a campaign has become a signal of craftsmanship, and the implication is clear: human-made art is seen as a sign of a premium brand.

A post shared by Ralph Lauren (@ralphlauren)

Apple's also been on the trend with its embroidered logo and the stop-motion ad for Apple Games, which was also made by Blinklink. The resurgence of interest in stop motion is likely to continue to grow with Laika's Wildwood doing well at the box office.

This week on Dezeen, architecture studio Foster + Partners and US studio Manica unveiled their design for Generali Stadium in Milan, which will become home to local football clubs AC Milan and Inter Milan.

The stadium will seat 71,500 people and be built alongside the 99-year-old San Siro stadium, which will eventually be torn down. Generali Stadium will be defined by a structural facade composed of elongated X-framed concrete supports.

Architect Norman Foster told Dezeen that the Generali Stadium’s design draws on his “great personal connection with the city”.

Foster also made the news this week with the launch of his first watch, which the architect designed for Spanish watch brand Lebond.

The watch draws on aviation design and was designed to be customised, in line with Foster’s philosophy that a watch is “intensely personal”.

The public vote winners for Dezeen Awards 2026 were announced this week and included Japanese studio Schemata Architects’ Uchida Shōten head office, above, in the architecture category.

We also revealed the public vote winners in the interiors and design categories. The public vote is separate from the main judging process, with the overall winners of this year’s programme set to be announced on 16 November.

In Abu Dhabi, a new concert hall by the late architect Frank Gehry was revealed. The Youth Orchestra Abu Dhabi will be located in the Mina Zayed port district.

It will be dedicated to young musicians and contain a 600-seat concert hall and 18 rehearsal rooms.

Technology brand Apple unveiled its new MacBook Pro model, which features its first-ever laptop touchscreen. The brand said the display is “a monumental step forward for the Mac”.

Apple Music also showed off a new logo this week. The first rebrand since Apple Music launched in 2015 was made in collaboration with musician Fred Again by passing sound waves through a pool of oil.

#8992. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

#8991. prince de conti hotel turns historic parisian interiors into theatrical guest rooms

set in saint-germain-des-prés, the 23-room boutique retreat blends rich tapestries, sumptuous fabrics and historical references with contemporary interiors inspired by 17th-century french elegance.

The Prince de Conti hotel reimagines a 17th-century Parisian building, infusing it with contemporary interior design within the historic Saint-Germain-des-Prés district. With just 23 rooms and suites, the four-star hotel has little interest in playing by the usual rules. Instead, it borrows the extravagance of its five-star counterparts, packing rich textures, theatrical details, and a healthy dose of 17th-century drama into a surprisingly intimate setting. Think less conventional hotel, more Parisian jewel box with a flair for the dramatic. Its prime location places it steps away from iconic landmarks such as Notre-Dame de Paris and the Hôtel de la Monnaie.

The Paristory group, a family-managed enterprise led by sisters Alexandra and Julie Marang, owns the Prince de Conti. This hotel marks a significant expansion for the group, as it is their first property situated on the Rive Gauche, a neighborhood holding personal significance for the Marang family. The group already operates three successful boutique hotels on the Rive Droite, bringing their expertise in hospitality and refined design to this new venture in the heart of Paris.

The interior design concept at the Prince de Conti draws extensively on historical references, which are carefully reinterpreted through a contemporary lens. The result is a playful mix of bold colors, historical motifs, and carefully chosen details, where the 17th century gets a contemporary makeover. Rather than recreating the past, the interiors borrow its most theatrical elements and give them a new role, creating spaces that feel somewhere between a private residence and a period drama, minus the powdered wigs.

The 17th century makes its presence felt throughout, with nods to the larger-than-life characters and events of the period. Rich wood finishes, elaborate tapestries, and sumptuous fabrics set the scene, borrowing a few tricks from the French aristocracy’s decorating playbook. Historical references are given a contemporary twist, bringing a touch of old-world extravagance into the present without turning the hotel into a museum.

No two rooms tell quite the same story. Each of the 23 rooms and suites is treated as a miniature stage set, with its own character, decorative details, and historical references. Theatrical touches abound, but the scale remains intimate, making the experience feel more like stepping into an eccentric private residence than checking into a conventional hotel.

That sense of informality extends to the hotel’s honesty bar, where guests can help themselves to wine, spirits, or other drinks and simply keep track of what they’ve had. No bartender, no elaborate rituals, just a little old-fashioned trust. It’s a refreshingly relaxed touch in a setting that otherwise takes its decorative drama rather seriously.

Most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate plan must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

Without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

Key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

A revocable living trust is the foundational estate planning tool for FIRE households. It provides three critical benefits that matter more for early retirees than conventional retirees:

Every early retiree needs three healthcare documents executed before leaving their employer:

Once you cross the $1 million net worth threshold — common in the FIRE community — asset protection becomes essential. You have decades of retirement ahead during which a lawsuit, car accident judgment, or liability claim could threaten the wealth you worked so hard to build.

For FIRE households pursuing charitable giving, a donor-advised fund (DAF) allows you to front-load charitable deductions in high-income years (or Roth conversion years), reduce your taxable estate, and distribute grants to charities over time. A DAF contribution is irrevocable and immediately reduces your estate while giving you advisory control over future grants.

Do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate plan. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

For most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

Yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Review your estate plan every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a new state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more important than for conventional retirees.

Estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate plan: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

Featuring an architect’s pink PoMo dreamhouse and a home for kids that looks like a wooden wardrobe, here are Dezeen’s houses of the month for October.

Our monthly roundup of the most popular residences featured on Dezeen captures everything from a bungalow conversion in northern England to super-luxe villas in Ibiza and Switzerland.

Read on to find out more about Dezeen readers’ favourite houses this month:

Architect Peter Morris wanted to give his “love of postmodernism a chance to reveal itself fully” with this pair of residences in north London, one inhabited by himself and his wife and another by a neighbour with similar tastes.

“The key goal was to make a beautiful building which I hoped might create a little moment of joy for anyone walking past it on the street,” Morris told Dezeen.

Wardrobe House, Czech Republic, by Šépka Architekti

As its name suggests, this house was intended to resemble a wooden wardrobe. Like a piece of flat-pack furniture, it was prefabricated as a kit of parts and assembled on-site.

Šépka Architekti designed the house for a couple who wanted to provide two of their teenage children with independent living space, and it sits in the garden of the main family home.

Bellavista 11, Spain, by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos

This luxurious villa steps down a hillside on the eastern coast of Ibiza in three low-slung volumes.

Designed by Valencian studio Fran Silvestre Arquitectos, it is unmistakably minimalist, made up of pared-back white concrete rectangles.

House on a Slope, Switzerland, by Think Architecture

An underground corridor (pictured left) connects the two parts of this house overlooking Lake Zurich, designed by Swiss studio Think Architecture.

The architects had been tasked with fitting a very large amount of floorspace onto a narrow, sloping site while being as sensitive as possible to the landscape.

Deyne Avenue extension, UK, by Loader Monteith

A two-bed bungalow in Prestwich has been transformed into a four-bedroom family home with only a modest expansion of its footprint by Scottish architecture practice Loader Monteith.

In what the studio described as “squeezing a quart into a pint pot”, a rear extension and dormer loft conversion were added, along with a reorganisation of the floor plan.

What do you mean Mr Monopoly doesn't have a monocle?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most of us have been playing Monopoly since we were kids, so it's one of the most recallable logos out there, right? Of course, I'm talking about Mr Monopoly, also known as Rich Uncle Pennybags, who is kitted out as a very fancy gentleman with a moustache, top hat, cane and monocle. Except he doesn't have a monocle. Seriously.

This is just one of the many logos subject to the Mandela effect, a psychological and social phenomenon that convinces us of visual elements that simply don't exist. A few years ago, we reported that scholars at the University of Chicago studied the effect and found that people share the same false memories of a range of logos and icons. The very best logos are memorable, but some of them have false additions in the minds of many people.

We decided to revisit this study after a chat in the office brought up the design details that actually don't exist in real life – and we want to know, have you been subject to the Mandela effect in these cases? If so, let us know in the comments. And if you have any other logos you've misremembered, can you draw your version and upload them in the comments?

Neuroscientist Wilma Bainbridge and lab manager Deepasri Prasad at the University of Chicago's Brain Bridge Lab found that people have confident and consistent false memories of famous icons. The team trawled internet discussions for logos and characters people commonly misremember, then added their own picks and made small tweaks to see if people could spot the real thing. In total there were 40 images, including the logos for Apple, Bic, Disney, Fruits of the Loom, Ralph Lauren and Volkswagen, plus the Bluetooth symbol, Pikachu, C-3PO, Wally and Curious George.

Participants had to pick the correct version from three options. Apple and Ralph Lauren did well, with around 80 per cent getting them right. Monopoly, Volkswagen and Fruits of the Loom did not: only 20 to 30 per cent chose the real logo. Most people also insisted Pikachu’s tail has a black tip. It doesn’t.

It wasn’t just a multiple-choice problem either. When asked to draw the images from memory, people made the same mistakes unprompted. Bainbridge says it’s a strong effect: people hold a false memory of an image they’ve never actually seen.

Nobody knows yet. The study doesn’t identify a cause. One suggestion is schema theory, where our brains add details that fit the theme. A monocle says ‘wealthy Victorian gent’, so in it goes.

Sign up to the design newsletter from Creative Bloq, brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of graphic design, branding, typography and more.

That doesn’t explain everything, though. A cornucopia isn’t an obvious addition to a plate of fruit, which is the problem with using schema theory to explain the Fruits of the Loom logo. (The scene does exist in art, but that’s a stretch.)

The researchers say the findings could matter for logo design and for choosing images in education and advertising, where accurate memory is the whole point. Bainbridge also linked it to wider questions about the images used in the media.

It’s a useful reminder that ‘memorable’ and ‘remembered correctly’ aren’t the same thing.

#8986. live-build documentary captures 1:1 timber pavilions at studio in the woods workshop

marking the 20th anniversary of studio in the woods, the documentary crossing, lookout, horizon chronicles the design and construction of three full-scale timber installations built from site-felled timber at the AA’s hooke park campus.

Rob Fiehn edited by christina vergopoulou November 4, 2026 4 min

Marking the 20th anniversary of the architectural live-build summer school Studio in the Woods (SiTW), a new documentary short titled Crossing, Lookout, Horizon records the initiative’s 2026 session hosted at the Architectural Association’s (AA) Hooke Park campus in Dorset, UK. Founded two decades ago by Piers Taylor of Invisible Studio alongside architects Meredith Bowles, Kate Darby, Gianni Botsford, and Peter Clegg, with early mentorship from Ted Cullinan, the program functions as a hands-on pedagogical alternative to traditional studio-based design education.

Operating without predetermined briefs, the annual workshop convenes roughly 50 students, practitioners, and timber specialists over an intensive four-day build cycle. Participants design and assemble 1:1 structural interventions using timber harvested and milled directly from the surrounding woodland. Sited within Hooke Park’s working forest, the 2026 iteration produced three site-specific timber installations, Crossing, Lookout, and Horizon, testing material optimization, reciprocal framing, and direct fabrication methods.

Across its twenty-year history, Studio in the Woods has convened a broad network of practitioners, structural engineers, and timber fabricators to lead its on-site workshops. The teaching roster includes Stirling Prize winner Niall McLaughlin, Lebanese-French architect Lina Ghotmeh, and collaborative design practice Architecture 00. Instruction pairs architectural theory with structural pragmatism through contributions from master timber framer Charley Brentnall, former Hooke Park director Martin Self, Lee Ivett of Baxendale, and structural engineers Tim Lucas (Price & Myers) and Toby McClean (Tall Engineers). Additional past workshop leaders include Akos Juhasz, Fergus Feilden of Feilden Fowles, Smith Mordak, Shin Egashira of the Architectural Association, Hannah Durham, Zoe Berman, and Je Ahn of Studio Weave. This multi-disciplinary teaching body grounds the program in a synthesis of structural calculation, joinery craft, and material testing directly in the field.

enjoying the ‘lookout’ structure firsthand

Parallel to the physical construction, the 2026 iteration integrated a specialized film mentorship program directed by architectural documentarians Nyima Murry and Jim Stephenson. Designed to lower barriers of entry into architectural cinematography for students from historically underrepresented backgrounds, an open call selected three architecture students with limited film experience: Tong Hao, Jaime Nelson, and Hamani Altraiji. Following technical modules on visual storytelling, equipment rigging, and sound recording, the fellows embedded within the Hooke Park working forest for four days. Working from a documentary brief devised by SiTW co-founder Piers Taylor of Invisible Studio, the film team tracked the live assembly of the three installations, Crossing, Lookout, and Horizon, recording structural trials, ambient woodland acoustics, and real-time timber manipulation to produce a permanent document of the collective live-build methodology.

#8985. O'Sullivan Skoufoglou Architects creates "quiet yet present" garden studio in London

A low brick base anchors the timber structure of this pared-back garden studio, which London studio O’Sullivan Skoufoglou Architects created as a workspace for a creative couple in Highbury.

Nestled in a leafy garden of a Victorian home, the studio provides the filmmaker and artist with a calming, well-lit space with a strong visual connection to the outdoors.

O’Sullivan Skoufoglou Architects slotted it at the end of the garden to preserve views from the house over the mature garden, avoiding “compromising the sense of depth and continuity of the landscape”, the studio said.

“It was important that the building felt distinct from the house while sitting comfortably within its setting, a short walk from the rear garden door,” studio co-founder Amalia Skoufoglou told Dezeen.

“The intention was to create a building that felt quiet yet present in the garden, rather than competing with it or the Victorian house,” she added.

“The form allows the quality of the space to emerge through its proportions, construction and relationship with daylight,” Skoufoglou continued. “Its modest scale and subservient position give the studio the character of a garden building.”

O’Sullivan Skoufoglou Architects designed the material palette and low profile of the studio to complement the character of the existing house and garden, ensuring minimal visual impact.

Its low brick plinth nods to the brick boundary walls of the Victorian home and also pays homage to Victorian glasshouses, traditionally supported on low brick walls.

Above the brick plinth is a lightweight timber structure, chosen to “allow the upper part of the building to remain visually light”, Skoufoglou said.

Inside, the garden studio comprises a main open workspace and an adjoining bathroom. The focal point is its built-in desk that extends along the main east-facing window wall.

“The main window wall and the built-in desk form the focus of the interior. The desk runs alongside the generous east-facing windows, making daylight and the changing garden views an integral part of the working environment,” said Skoufoglou.

“This arrangement brings the working surface into direct relationship with natural light and views of the garden.”

Inside, the timber structure is left exposed at roof level, while the brick plinth is also left visible. Between, the walls are lined with painted pine.

According to the studio, the “grain of the timber, the texture of the brick and the changing daylight combine to give the space its character”.

Other London garden studios featured on Dezeen include Shou Sugi Bangers, a timber music studio by Unknown Works, and Gardenhide Studio, a hempcrete workspace by Commonbond Architects.

#8984. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

The retro board-game-and-video-game hybrid just got a major price drop.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Board is a new 24-inch touchscreen console that swaps controllers for chunky physical board game pieces and has had a teasing price cut ahead of Black Friday. Board is now $339.15 on Amazon, down from its $399 list price.

This isn't a big-screen game console; it's a mix of board gaming and retro tabletop bar video games. The flat-lying 24-inch touchscreen tracks the physical pieces you slide, spin and pick up. Includes the co-op cooking game Chop Chop and the six-game Retro Arcade Collection.

Those seven games and pieces are essentially modern takes on Asteroids, plus Chop Chop is a co-op culinary party game in the vein of Overcooked. You can expand your library with additional packs, but there's no subscription, and you can buy extras one at a time.

As the name suggests, Board is a 24-inch tabletop touchscreen console that uses physical pieces as controllers. Its PieceSense tech tracks each piece’s position and movement, blending board-game fun with video games, entirely subscription-free.

The 24-inch anti-glare screen suits families and groups, with solo, co-op and competitive modes. There’s Wi-Fi 6 and 64GB of storage under the woodgrain-effect frame. It ticks my need for a new way to play games, feels retro and modern all at once, and I can see the family loving this like they do Nex Playground, particularly as some of the games feature party play and Tamagotchi ideas – Mushka is a little dog that lives inside Board and can be played with.

The pieces are the smart idea here. Board’s PieceSense tech identifies each piece, where it is, and how it’s moving, so kids who’d fumble a standard controller can pick up a plastic spaceship and fly it straight away. That active interaction gives Board an old-fashioned Nintendo appeal.

The Signature Game Collection pack, Board’s five most popular games, is 20% off. Games include Save the Bloogs, Sushi Duel Omakase, Spycraft, the digital pet Mushka, and the block-stacking Strata & Daily Build.

Save 20% on the newest game collection – Board’s Summer Game Collection adds three new games with physical pieces: the mirror-bending puzzler The Heist, the treasure-hunting Bloogs Blitz, and a 3-in-1 sports game bundle covering Golf, Pool, and Bowling.

#8982. pixelated ceramic tiles and folded aluminum compose electrical substation’s facade in virginia

atelier manferdini wraps the crystal substation in arlington, with invisible, an infrastructural facade that pairs generative ceramic tilework and folded anodized aluminum panels with programmable RGB LEDs.

E. Manferdini edited by christina vergopoulou November 4, 2026 3 min

Designed by Atelier Manferdini, inVisible is an architectural envelope intervention that wraps Dominion Energy’s Crystal Substation at the corner of South Hayes Street and South Fern Street in Arlington County, Virginia. Developed as part of an infrastructural upgrade to replace aging equipment, increase capacity, and support rising energy demand in National Landing, the project conceals utilitarian power conversion equipment behind a multi-layered civic facade composed of custom ceramic tilework, folded aluminum rainscreens, and programmable LED lighting systems.

The exterior envelope is bifurcated into two horizontal zones that contrast in material, texture, and visual weight. The lower plinth features glazed ceramic tiles in three modular dimensions, 2, 4, and 6 inches, designed by Atelier Manferdini to visually reflect internal step-down voltage conversions. Clad in a ten-hue gradient palette, the tiling layout was generated using custom scripts in the Processing creative coding environment, which introduced synthetic visual glitching patterns that suggest dynamic electrical currents. Above this pixelated ceramic datum, the upper band consists of folded, monochromatic anodized aluminum panels. The angular origami-like folds catch daylight and cast shifting shadows across the metallic skin throughout the diurnal cycle. After dark, integrated RGB LED arrays wash across both materials, modulating light intensity and color temperature to animate the perimeter of the civic utility site.

#8981. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.
