Most U.S. airline loyalty programs use region-based or dynamic pricing for award flights, charging the same number of miles whether you fly 200 miles or 2,000. British Airways uses distance-based pricing instead, which means shorter flights cost dramatically fewer Avios. Since BA is a Oneworld partner with American Airlines, you can use Avios to book AA-operated nonstop domestic flights. The result: a flight that AA might price at 12,500-25,000 miles can be booked for just 7,500 Avios through BA. This is one of the most reliable and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards.

Sign up for a free BA Executive Club account at ba.com. This is where your Avios balance lives and where you will search and book award flights on American Airlines.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant. Only transfer what you need for a specific booking.

On the BA website, search for your route using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for American Airlines-operated nonstop flights. Filter results to find flights coded as AA with available Avios seats.

Confirm the flight is pricing at 7,500 Avios (under 1,151 miles) or 10,000 Avios (1,151-2,000 miles). Check that taxes and fees are the expected $5.60. If prices seem high, try different dates or check that you selected a nonstop flight.

Book the flight and add your AAdvantage number to the reservation so you receive any applicable elite benefits. You will receive a confirmation from British Airways, and the ticket will also appear in your AA account.

Yes. British Airways and American Airlines are both Oneworld alliance members, so you can use BA Avios to book award seats on AA-operated flights. You book directly through the British Airways website (ba.com) and search for AA flight numbers.

Flights under 1,151 miles cost 7,500 Avios each way in economy. Flights between 1,151-2,000 miles cost 10,000 Avios. Flights between 2,001-3,000 miles cost 12,500 Avios. The value proposition is strongest on the shortest flights where the Avios cost is lowest.

Not on domestic American Airlines flights. The typical fee is just $5.60 each way. High fuel surcharges only apply when booking British Airways-operated long-haul flights, not when using Avios on partner airlines like AA domestically.

Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to British Airways Avios. Transfer ratios are 1:1 from Chase, Amex, and Capital One. Transfers are typically instant or within 24 hours.

This sweet spot was practically designed for the ChooseFI beginner — someone who has their first transferable points card (a Chase Sapphire Preferred, an Amex Gold, or a Bilt card) and wants to make a real, tangible redemption without navigating complex routing rules or praying for elusive premium cabin availability.

Minimum to get started: You need at least 7,500 Avios (or transferable points to convert) for a one-way. For a round-trip, 15,000. Most sign-up bonuses — even modest ones — cover multiple round-trips with this sweet spot.

Who this is NOT for: If you're flying coast-to-coast (NYC to LAX is over 2,400 miles — a different, higher Avios tier), this specific pricing won't apply. This sweet spot is purpose-built for short hops under 650 miles. It's also not the move if you already have AA elite status and can snag cheap upgrades — but for the rest of us, it's perfect.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness** — and that rating is fully deserved. Let's be specific about why. The hardest part of most award bookings is finding available seats and navigating confusing partner systems. This one simplifies both: you're searching a major U.S. airline's (AA) domestic saver inventory, which is widely available on popular short-haul routes year-round. You're not hunting for a specific aircraft with lie-flat seats or hoping a single partner releases one business class seat. Domestic economy saver space is genuinely accessible. The booking process itself is two websites: aa.com to check availability, britishairways.com to book. Neither requires a phone call, neither has complicated routing rules for simple one-way or round-trip domestic bookings, and the transfer from Chase or Amex is instant. **The three things to get right:** 1. **Confirm saver availability on AA before transferring** — This habit protects you from the only real risk (irreversible point transfers). 2. **Verify the operating carrier is American Airlines, not British Airways** — One glance at 'Operated by' in the booking details handles this. 3. **Keep your BA Executive Club account active** — Set a reminder to log in or earn at least once every 36 months so your Avios don't expire. That's genuinely the whole checklist. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is the redemption to start with. You'll build the muscle memory — search, confirm, transfer, book — in about 20 minutes, and you'll have a nearly free flight to show for it. Welcome to travel rewards.

Using British Airways Avios for short domestic nonstop flights on American Airlines is one of the most practical and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards. At just 7,500 Avios each way with $5.60 in fees, it dramatically undercuts what AA charges through its own program. With four major transfer partners feeding BA Avios, this sweet spot is accessible from virtually any points-earning strategy. Whether you are booking a quick NYC-Chicago hop or an LA-San Francisco shuttle, BA Avios should be your first look for short-haul domestic flights.

#8929. Ultimate Guide to 4A Hair: Care Tips, Styles, and Maintenance

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

Alright, curl friends, let’s break it down. Hair type falls into four main categories:

Now, Type 4 hair is where things get seriously curly and coily. Within this category, we’ve got subtypes A, B, and C,

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Yes, 4A hair is curly and falls under the coily category. It features tight, springy curls that form an S-shape.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Love those natural curls — keep them hydrated, avoid excessive heat, and give them some nighttime TLC.

How we reported this: Editor-in-chief Chris Foster has spent hundreds of hours using these watches for training, everyday wear, and nighttime metrics. Foster has independently tested nearly every smartwatch/GPS watch that’s been released in the last eight years, and draws on a decade of making a living as a pro triathlete to inform his impressions. The brands provide all watches on loan.

If you’re a triathlete in the market for a smartwatch or GPS watch, the options just keep getting better. Some of the best triathlon watches in 2026 are getting cheaper, and high-end features that used to cost over $800 are coming down into the $400 range.

What is the only differentiator between a good GPS watch for triathletes and a great one in 2026? It boils down to which is easiest to use, which has those sneaky features you didn’t know you needed, and what you’re (actually) going to do with it.

Below we’ve got brand-new, editor-tested smartwatches and GPS watches from Suunto, Apple, Coros, Amazfit, and Garmin that have all been released in fall 2026. Our editors spend hours training and sleeping with these watches to see what works as advertised, what provides the most accurate (and useful) information, and if it’s intuitive or not.

We review these through the lens of a triathlete who trains multiple times per week, wants to know how their body is reacting to their training, and relies on the data and information for important training and racing decisions. Read on for our expert impressions.

We’ve also included a “Where does it stand?” section for each watch to help you understand where it fits in today’s smartwatch universe. And if you want to dig deeper, we’ve got links to longer reviews for most of the watches below.

Looking for an older smartwatch? We don’t miss much, so check out our previous roundups for quick looks and deep dives on watches from previous years, like the Garmin Fenix 8 or the Suunto Race S – take a look at the 2024 roundup for more.

We’ve also got watches from 2023, like the Polar Pacer, Coros Apex 2 Pro, Garmin Forerunner 965, Suunto 9 Peak Pro, Apple Watch Ultra 1, and Garmin Enduro 2. Or watches from 2022, like the Timex R300, Wahoo Rival, Apple Watch Series 7, Garmin Instinct 2 Solar, Polar Grit X Pro, Suunto 9 Peak, Coros Vertix 2, and Garmin Fenix 7X Solar. Or our 2020 buyer’s guide with reviews of the Coros Pace 2, Apple Watch SE, Garmin Forerunner 745, Fitbit Sense, Polar Vantage V2, and Suunto 7.

The Suunto Race 3S is the little cousin of a slightly larger (but cheaper) Race 2. The Race 3S has a 1.32-inch AMOLED touchscreen that maxes out at 2,000 nits, with 45 hours of multi-band GPS and 64GB of offline mapping and music storage. Like the Race 2, it has sapphire crystal glass, but unlike the Race 2, it weighs in at around 56g compared to the Race 2’s beefy 76g.

The specs are pretty much what you’d expect for a watch in the $400-600 price range, and in real-life testing, the Race 3S also felt nearly identical to the brand-new $400 Suunto Run 2, which was just released about a month ago: They look nearly the same, they feel, weigh, and perform pretty much exactly the same, but the Run 2 only has 24 hours of multi-band GPS and 10 days of advertised daily use (though we found less than that, closer to right days). That said, the Run 2 is $200 cheaper than the Race 3S, so you’re basically paying $200 for a little more battery life, but materially not much else.

While the Race 3S is a fine smartwatch out of context, once you put it up against other smartwatches in the $400-600 range, it struggles a little bit to find its place. First, the elephant in the room is that the Suunto Race 2 has more battery life (and a bigger screen, for better or for worse) for less money. In some ways, the Race 3S is more like a Race 2S, especially given that it’s almost unfair to compare the Race 3S to the original Race S that was released two years ago. But even then, if this was a Race 2S (which it’s not), you’d really have to want a slightly smaller watch to spend less money on an arguably better watch in the Race 2.

The next problem for the Race 3S is also competition from the $400 Run 2, which still isn’t my favorite watch of the year, simply because of the biggest issue Suunto has here: the presence of the $450 Coros Pace 4 Pro. The Pace 4 Pro costs (way) less than the Race 3S, has a bigger screen, weighs slightly less, and has about the same battery life.

The other competition in this price range – watches like the Garmin Forerunner 570 ($550) or the $500 Polar Vantage M3 don’t really overpower the Race 3S, but they’re also not obviously a worse choice. That said, if you put the Race 3S up against Suunto’s own $600 Vertical 2 – with much more battery life, a bigger screen, and an awesome LED flashlight, it’s not even a fair fight. I’d easily spend another $100 for that watch, but it’s the same price.

That said, I’m not sure exactly who the Suunto Race 3S is for. It faces stiff competition from older Suunto watches, like the Race 2 or the Vertical 2, and it struggles mightily against watches like the Coros Pace 4 Pro, or even the $250 Coros Pace 4 (if size/weight truly is your goal and you really need a smaller, ultra-lightweight watch with just enough features and onboard mapping).

The Coros Pace 4 Pro is the latest in one of my favorite lines of endurance-focused smartwatches. Beginning with the almost-too-cheap Pace 2, Coros has taken chunks out of the smartwatch market with a super lightweight and entirely capable offering that doesn’t break the bank. Released less than a year ago, the Pace 4 was arguably one of the best smartwatches for the money, and it was hard to imagine what could come next.

But here we are with the Pace 4 Pro, boasting a big, bright 37.3mm screen with a blinding 3,500nits. This is a big deal because in bright sunlight, if you’re actually using the 32GB of onboard navigation, you need a big screen to see it all, and it needs to be bright enough to see in direct sunlight. Pair those features with the digital dial (essential for zooming navigation on the go, in my opinion), and you’ve already got a best-in-class watch for routing and mapping. All for $450.

Past that, at 51g plus a super-thin side profile, the Pace 4 Pro disappears on one’s wrist in a way that very few watches with these features do. For those of us with small wrists (or those of us who struggle to remove a wetsuit quickly over their watch), this is a big deal.

If there’s room to complain, the only caveat with the Pace 4 Pro is that the styling is still extremely sporty, and the design doesn’t really lend itself to all-day wear. The titanium case and sapphire glass do help with durability, but I still maintain that the aesthetic isn’t quite there on the mid-to-lower end of the Coros line.

All in all, the Coros Pace 4 Pro is a strong contender for the best watch of the year, especially in the highly competitive $400-600 price range (more on that below), and you’d have a hard time feeling limited with this watch.

First it’s worth noting that the $400-600 price range is by far the most competitive in sport-focused smartwatches. For $450 you can get pretty much everything you used to find on a $1,000 watch — and in many cases these less-expensive models are better than the top of the pile just a few years ago.

The $450 Coros Pace 4 Pro most squarely competes with the Garmin Forerunner 570 ($550), the Polar Vantage M3 ($500), the Coros Apex 2 ($480), the Suunto Race 2 ($500), and the Suunto Vertical 2 ($600). You could also include the new Suunto Run 2 ($350), but I don’t think that’s a fair fight.

To my mind, only the Suunto Race 2 and the Suunto Vertical 2 truly compete because the Forerunner 570 costs more and has way less battery (and a smaller screen), the Polar has a host of issues, and the Apex 2’s screen isn’t even in the same league as the Pace 4 Pro.

When squared up against the Suunto Race 2, you’re spending $50 more for a watch with slightly worse battery life, a similarly sized screen (though not as bright as the Pace 4 Pro), but arguably better styling. The Race 2 is also heavier (by a bit) and bulkier.

When up against the Vertical 2, the Suunto easily wins on battery life and the not-to-be-ignored LED flashlight (early morning transitions anyone?) with a similarly sized screen, but it’s a chunker to be sure and costs $100 more — it also lacks a digital dial, which hurts its nav use more than you’d think.

To me, it’s a toss-up between the three, but if money is an object and style is not, the fantastic Coros Pace 4 Pro is the winner.

When the first Apple Watch Ultra was released back in 2022, the big tagline (for triathletes, anyway) was: The First Apple Watch That Can Do An Ironman. It was notable because Apple’s previous smartwatches were so heavy on lifestyle features and light on battery power that you literally couldn’t complete a 10-15-hour Ironman wearing one — even if you felt the sports features were robust enough to be helpful, which they weren’t at the time.

In the years since, Apple has consistently produced one of the prettiest, brightest, fastest, and most feature-packed smartwatches for 80% of the population, but even the Ultra line struggled to stand out — especially as the Ultra line made minor changes from version to version: The Ultra 2 brightened the screen, which was nice; the 3 added satellite emergency SOS and a sweeter screen, but almost nothing else. To the latter upgrades, I still maintain that relying on any smartwatch for SOS/satellite comms in the backcountry over a dedicated device like an inReach or even your phone is a very narrow use case and feels extremely reckless, but that’s just me.

But now enter the Ultra 4, which in my opinion is the most relevant upgrade for triathletes since the first version leapt above the Watch Series line. The Ultra 4 has all of the above upgrades but adds some of the most sensitive and accurate heart-rate sensing/physio tracking that I’ve ever used (this is good news for triathletes).

After testing a load of smartwatches this year with sleep tracking that ranges from “good enough” to “seriously I’ve been awake for hours,” only the Ultra 4’s “Overnight Vitals” syncs up with my true sleep cycles and accurately flagged a bad infection that was developing in my leg. I wasn’t even experiencing fever or any outward effects, but the thoughtful (and easy-to-use) combination of very accurate heart rate, accurate sleep cycles, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and HRV detected the rise and fall of the infection.

I was similarly impressed with the readiness app that helped guide my activity based on vitals and previous activities. Sure, almost every other endurance-focused smartwatch has these features, but none are as accurate and easy to digest.

The last note may seem minor, but it’s not: With the slight increase in battery life, you can now make it through two sleeps before recharging, which means you’re less likely to have to charge overnight or miss/delay a workout while it charges. Yes, 2-3 days is still like 1/8th of most endurance-focused smartwatches, but giving yourself two nights (and a speedier charger that gives you 18 hours in only 15 minutes), it’s finally usable for daily multisport wear and training.

So when you look at the $800-$1,000 price range, you’re looking at smartwatches that do everything and last forever. Up against the $1,000 Garmin Fenix 9, for instance, you’ve got satellite/SOS comms (like the Ultra 4), an AMOLED touchscreen, and pretty much everything else a smartwatch can do — including things like offline voice commands, hands-free calling, an LED flashlight, and more. Most crucially, you’re also getting two weeks or more of battery life to the Ultra 4’s 2-3 days.

That said, if you’re an iPhone user, there is a host of connectivity and lifestyle features that are truly enhanced by the Ultra 4. You can respond to texts, Slacks, sync up everyday mapping and navigation (like when you’re driving around), and way more. No Garmin device (or any other brand) does that with Apple smartphones.

However, if you’re an Android user, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is wildly overpriced and underpowered because it won’t connect at all with your device (Garmin et al. will). Looking down into the super-competitive $600-ish price range, I’d recommend buyers strongly compare the Ultra 4 to the $600 Suunto Vertical 2 thanks to its LED flashlight and exceptional mapping and battery life. I’d also consider the way overfeatured (almost to a fault) and battery-heavy $650 Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar.

Ever since I noticed 2025 UTMB race winner Ruth Croft’s Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro on her wrist a year ago in Chamonix, France, my interest in China-based Amazfit was rekindled. I did a handful of tests on their early endurance-focused efforts, and I felt them to be so beta that I passed on reviewing their models for a few years. Since the T-Rex 3 Pro, however, I’ve kept my eyes peeled for another model that might be interesting for triathletes.

The T-Rex Dual Solar certainly met those standards, with a built-in LED flashlight (think: early morning transition areas or dawn/dusk patrol runs), a surprisingly fast AMOLED (and very bright) screen, enough battery life to get past my magic two-week benchmark, and an almost-ludicrous amount of features, on the same level as a Garmin Fenix, but for at least 30% less money.

First, let’s talk about the most obvious feature on this watch: the dual-sided solar panels. Yes, it seems goofy to have solar panels on the back of the watch, but there are absolutely situations where you might want to try to top up (or at least drain slower) your battery life. I would say in backpacking, this use case comes up pretty often. In triathlon training/life, probably less so: If you’re taking off your watch, you might as well charge the thing, which is infinitely faster than even the best wrist-top solar panels. That said, it is a neat little gimmick.

More importantly, the T-Rex Dual Solar is $150 more than the surprisingly capable T-Rex 3 Pro, but the former doesn’t have a ton more than the latter. Both have two-week-ish battery life, a speaker and microphone, an LED flashlight, rugged styling/durability, and a nearly nauseating host of features — of which a handful are materially useful.

We’re in a time when very few watches do much more than others — with the exception of LED flashlights (which I think are super helpful for triathletes), voice inputting (a mic), and onboard satellite/SOS comms (which I think aren’t that helpful). The T-Rex Dual Solar does everything in that list, except the last, which I don’t find much of a use case for. So then you have to ask, does it do all of those things well? And, are those things easy to use? In the case of the T-Rex Dual Solar, the answer is kind of. User interface and bus were always a little bit of a problem with the first run of Amazfit watches, and while this round is way better, they’re still not as intuitive as a Garmin, Coros, or Apple — the three major competitors.

All that said, if you love a bottomless hole of features, strong battery, LED flashlight, and voice features/functions but don’t want to spend more than $700 and don’t care about a hefty weight and giant wrist footprint, this is it — unless of course you’re good with the T-Rex 3 Pro.

In the $600-plus price range, which I consider the premium range of smartwatches, there’s some pretty tough competition for the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar. First, you have the $800 Apple Watch Ultra 4, which gets blown out of the water by the battery life on the T-Rex Solar (and has no LED flashlight), but crushes the Amazfit when it comes to usability and lifestyle features (though irrelevant if you don’t own an iPhone). The latest Ultra also crushes the T-Rex Dual Solar in terms of 24/7 health metrics and physio measuring/monitoring accuracy; the Ultra 4 also has that standalone satellite/SOS comms, and the Amazfit definitely does not.

Above that, the Garmin Fenix 9 comes in around $1,000 and has pretty much everything that the Ultra 4 does, plus an LED flashlight and enough battery life to put up a fight against the T-Rex Dual Solar (though the Garmin would still lose). The Garmin, however, is far more intuitive and easy to use than the Amazfit, and its host of excellent apps (like Spotify, for instance) make it a clear winner. For a Garmin closer in price, the $750 Forerunner 970 also mirrors the T-Rex Dual Solar’s capabilities with easier interfaces (but less battery).

Looking below that, the $400-600 range is also pretty dangerous — especially Amazfit’s own fully capable $400 Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro that’s virtually identical to the T-Rex Dual Solar if you’re not making lots of use of the backside solar panel. Other than that, there are super capable LED flashlight-equipped watches like the Suunto Vertical 2 ($600) that offer much easier-to-use functions with better companion apps.

There was a time when the Garmin Fenix was pricey, but not out of reach. Less than five years ago you could find a brand-new Fenix 7 for $700. The battery would last close to forever, and there was a chance you’d never use half of the features packed into it. For another $100 or so you could get that all-valuable LED flashlight that used to be unique to the line, but now exists on less-expensive Garmin Instincts, the Suunto Vertical 2, and a few models from Amazfit. You’d get a lot for under $1,000, but you’d still probably not use close to all of it.

Fast forward to today, and the least-expensive Fenix 9 is $1,000. Garmin has added an AMOLED screen to some (and significantly lessened battery life on those models), a speaker/mic, faster map processing, and inReach comm options. If you’re really trying to do an apples-to-apples comparison, the 2022 Fenix 7X Pro Solar ($900 when released) and the 2026 Fenix 9 Pro Solar ($1,300) both have MIP screens and big battery life, but the latter has a mic/speaker (and all that comes with it, like voice control), inReach capabilities built in, and more storage/faster processing. With that in mind (and with the added $8/mo+ cost of the inReach plan), triathletes need to be very thoughtful about how they’re actually going to use the Fenix 9.

Since the inReach capabilities are the newest, shiniest thing across the full Fenix 9 line (and the subscription cost isn’t nothing), triathletes need to think about how often they’d go into an off-grid situation without a smartphone — or actual inReach. If you’re venturing into the rugged backcountry for days on end, you should really arm yourself with a dedicated inReach device, like the $300 Messenger. If you’re not going out for multiple days, most Apple phones now have similar sat features. Barring that, do you really need a no-phone, no-inReach device smartwatch? Probably not.

InReach notwithstanding, the Fenix 9 series feels less novel than it used to be for much more than it used to cost; in the context of the mish-mash featured Fenix 8 line — that had inReach functionality on some models, super-bright MicroLED on others — it feels a little redundant. Of course it has a styling, durability, and construction that Fenix fans will naturally gravitate toward, but at over $1,000 it’s becoming a smaller club than it was.

If we’re looking solely at the MIP-screened (meaning not AMOLED, to be clear) solar version Fenix 9 Pro Solar that costs $1,300, you’re in rare air. None of the Fenix 8s (which are nearly identical to the rest of the Fenix 9 series in many ways) have an MIP screen, so you have to go up against some of the (discounted to under $800) Fenix 7Xs that don’t have inReach. In other brands, you’d be talking about the super long-in-the-tooth $600 Coros Vertix 2 with MIP and a bananas amount of battery, but no LED flashlight or inReach, but an arguably better digital dial for offline mapping use.

The only other watch that’s worth mentioning here is the $800 Apple Watch Ultra 4 that interestingly has onboard SOS/satellite capabilities but also a highly advanced AMOLED touchscreen and nearly incomparable battery life. Even if you look at the AMOLED versions of the Fenix 9 Series that start at $1,000, the Garmins are still blowing the doors off the battery life of the Ultra 4; the Apple claps back with vastly superior lifestyle features (for iPhone users) and a mic/speaker.

All that said, if you can live without inReach (like 99.9% of triathletes can) and a mic/speaker isn’t meaningful to you, now you’re looking at watches for easily half the price, making the whole value proposition pretty tough to stomach. Even the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar mentioned here adds a (not-as-good) mic/speaker and has an LED flashlight for $650.

*Tri Battery Life includes the following settings/uses: Always-on display with the lowest possible brightness for bright daylight use; sleep and all-day heart-rate tracking; HRV tracking; 1-2 workouts/day with max GPS accuracy.

#8927. Yinka Ilori reveals Tottenham Hotspur away shirt

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has collaborated with Premier League football team Tottenham Hotspur to create a customised version of the club’s colourful away shirt.

Ilori reimagined the colourful away shirt, which has a pattern with “never-before-seen visuals inspired by never-before-seen destinations”, by adding a graphic to the front and back.

On the front, in the position the sponsor logo is usually located, Ilori designed a circular motif combining the football club’s initials – THFC – with an abbreviation for London and the postcode for Tottenham, LDN17.

The lettering is bright orange with a white background.

On the rear of the shirt, Ilori created a graphic in his typical playful style around the letters COYS, which stands for Come On You Spurs.

Encircling the letters are the words “I know I am, I’m sure I am”, with the words “We are Tottenham wherever we go” around the whole graphic.

All of the lettering uses Ilori’s custom typeface, which was designed by type foundry British Standard Type for the designer in 2024.

According to the designer, who grew up in north London where the Populous-designed Tottenham Hotspur stadium is located, the collaboration aims to demonstrate the power of football to unite people.

“This project is a celebration of belonging and the power of football to bring people together,” said Ilori.

“For me, football is about the wider culture and the incredible sense of unity that comes from standing on the terraces, chanting alongside thousands of others,” he continued.

“I wanted the design to honour Tottenham Hotspur’s heritage while capturing that collective joy and spirit. The ‘Never Far From Home’ message really resonated with me, reflecting how football has the power to make you feel at home, wherever you are.”

The shirt is the latest design from the designer who has recently collaborated with brands including Brabantia and Veuve Clicquot.

Ilori also recently created a homeware and furniture collection for department store Dunelm.

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

#8926. What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

When I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a new wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

There’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz says.

It seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

Fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” says Fertz. “You are born young.”

It turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

Sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky says. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”

At school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

Research shows that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

“I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”

Even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

Italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

“Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”

Paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very important to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

At cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

In fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in New York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert says. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

The antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

In Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

“Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo says. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”

Indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

Italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

“The most important thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz says. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, plan outings, and get out of the house.”

According to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz says, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”

#8925. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

#8924. Former workshop converted into contemporary Japanese home with "a sense of the passage of time"

Japanese studio Akio Isshiki Architects has transformed the home and workshop of a sheet-metal craftsperson in the castle town of Tatsuno into a modern house with a latticed wooden gate.

Architect Akio Isshiki, the founder of the eponymous studio, said he had to take a lot of different aspects into consideration when designing the project.

Among them was the location, as the two-storey home is located in a historic town known for being built around a medieval mountain castle.

“The project explores an architecture that responds naturally to the many contexts and conditions surrounding the house: the historic streetscape of the former castle town, traces of the former owner’s work as a sheet-metal craftsman, the client’s wishes, and practical constraints such as building regulations and structural requirements,” Isshiki told Dezeen.

For example, while the client had initially wanted a deck that would be connected to the dining room, the compact site made such a design difficult.

Instead, Isshiki removed part of the existing interior of the dining room to create a terrace space, which also includes a traditional-style engawa platform to connect the home with the garden.

Here, the studio added a sliding glass door that was designed so that its frame is hidden in the wall when it is closed, creating the impression of a fully open space.

Isshiki also wanted the 144-square-metre contemporary home to nod to more traditional Japanese houses.

“To sit comfortably within the townscape that retains the character of a former castle town, the spatial principles of traditional machiya – Japanese old townhouses – have been incorporated into this contemporary residence,” he explained.

“Examples include a long approach leading towards a bright garden at the back of the house, and an engawa, a narrow platform that connects the interior with the garden.”

The former workshop in front of the house was treated as a public-facing space. Where it looks onto the street, Isshiki added a large latticed, sliding gate, made from cedar, as well as a narrow entrance porch.

Inside, this multi-functional space becomes almost like an enclosed terrace. Here, Isshiki also added a small wooden toilet, inspired by those found in traditional machiya houses.

The studio kept a number of objects that were found in the old workshop, including a metal ring that now decorates a handrail next to the indoor staircase.

Isshiki relocated this staircase so that it sits at the front of the house, in the old workshop space – one of the biggest changes made to the layout of the house. A stone underneath the first step provides a space to remove footwear.

Isshiki’s studio used wood throughout the renovation, as the original building was made from timber and this material worked best with the existing neighbourhood, including a historic shrine that stands directly across from the house.

“The newly added wood, including the doors, is cedar, which is also the primary wood used in the original structure,” Isshiki said.

“Cedar is one of the most widely used types of wood in Japan and is readily available,” he continued.

“The contrast between the lighter new cedar and the existing cedar, which has darkened with age, brings a sense of the passage of time to the house.”

Akio Isshiki Architects also used earthen plasterwork in the home to create a tactile feel, while Tunisian tiles add decorative patterns in the kitchen. Here, the studio also created a built-in, combined wooden dining table and work surface.

On the top floor, which has a bedroom, living room and guest room, the studio mostly kept the original layout.

However, it added a sunken study space and a tokonoma, a recessed area used to display flowers and pieces of art.

“Through careful consideration of spatial dimensions, light, connections to the outdoors, materials, details, and relationships between spaces, the aim was to create a home that feels comfortable as a whole,” Isshiki concluded about the renovation.

His studio has previously designed a charred-cedar-clad house in Osaka and married old and new within a combined home and restaurant.

#8923. 6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

These days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better. And you’re not imagining things: Half of adults and one-third of children in the United States take supplements regularly, according to the Office of Dietary Supplements.

Supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise. First, most physicians recommend obtaining nutrients directly from food rather than a pill or capsule. Second, supplements aren’t reviewed for safety and effectiveness by the FDA before they hit shelves. Because of all the concerns surrounding supplements, Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, a general internist and professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, takes a dim view of the category overall: In fact, “a vast majority of supplements are probably worthless,” he tells SELF.

Still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different. Many experts, as it turns out, do take some type of supplement, but they are choosy about which ones they select. Read on to learn more about six they actually use.

How it works: Vitamin D plays key roles in bone health and immune function. In fact, low vitamin D is associated with a wide swath of medical conditions, according to Dr. Linder—including cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and cardiovascular issues (and, famously, seasonal affective disorder, or SAD).

Why some docs like it: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, especially among people who live at northern latitudes that don’t see as much sun during the winter, and people with darker skin. What’s more, few foods contain significant amounts of vitamin D, so it’s tough to source enough from your diet. Lawrence Green, MD, a dermatologist and clinical professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, tells SELF that these two factors make vitamin D a rare nutrient “we do need to take supplements for.” Nearly every single one of the eight doctors who spoke with SELF for this article said they take a vitamin D supplement, especially in the winter, though the frequency and dosage varied.

What to keep in mind: Most docs recommend vitamin D3 (also known as cholecalciferol) over vitamin D2 (also known as ergocalciferol), as studies have shown that D3 is more effective at raising vitamin D levels in your blood. Whichever option you decide on, try to take it with food—specifically, an item that contains fat. Because vitamin D is a fat-soluble nutrient, it “absorbs better that way,” Sara Velayati, MD, an obesity medicine specialist at Montefiore Einstein and an assistant professor at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York City, tells SELF. For this reason, Dr. Green makes a point of taking his supplements with breakfast or dinner. “The fattier and thicker the meal,” the better, he says.

What it does: Calcium is a mineral that helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth. Women in their 40s approaching menopausal age should make it a particular priority to ensure their intake is adequate, Rachel Pessah-Pollack, MD, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health and a clinical professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, tells SELF, as the physical changes that come with perimenopause and menopause can heighten bone loss and downstream health conditions like osteoporosis.

Who takes it: Like the other supplements on this list, calcium is best sourced from your diet, Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. “But if you’re not able to (I try to get dairy products but often come up short), a supplement is needed.” She takes a combined calcium and vitamin D tablet daily, as vitamin D helps calcium absorb.

How to take it: “The type of calcium supplements you are taking matters,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are the two most common. “Calcium carbonate should be taken with food because it requires gastric acid to be absorbed,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium citrate is an alternative that can be taken with or without food.

How it works: Magnesium is a mineral that can enhance sleep and muscle recovery. Research has also shown that it’s effective at preventing migraines, Raquel Zemtsov, MD, MPH, a family medicine doctor and assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, tells SELF.

Why some docs like it: In addition to Dr. Zemtsov, who takes magnesium to stave off migraine symptoms, Dr. Velayati takes magnesium for the sleep benefits. Likewise, Sheeva Talebian, MD, a reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of New York, and Kathleen Jordan, MD, an internal medicine physician and chief medical officer at Midi Health, also turn to it at bedtime to boost their shut-eye.

What to keep in mind: Some types of magnesium are better tolerated, says Dr. Velayati—something to note if you’re especially sensitive to side effects. Magnesium glycinate “avoids the gastrointestinal upset caused by magnesium oxides and magnesium citrates,” for example, Dr. Jordan says. Depending on your needs, however, magnesium glycinate might not be the best option: Magnesium oxide is the recommended magnesium type for migraines, so that’s the one Dr. Zemtsov keeps on hand, for example. Taking magnesium with food can also help prevent GI distress, according to Dr. Velayati.

How it works: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats that are important for cardiovascular health. Common omega-3 supplements include fish oil and krill oil.

Why some docs like it: Dr. Jordan, Dr. Talebian, and Dr. Velayati all take omega-3s. “With their anti-inflammatory properties and association with improved brain health, this is a popular supplement among physicians, myself included,” Dr. Jordan, who takes krill oil, says. Similarly, Dr. Velayati dabbles in fish oil, but takes it selectively. “The right dose really depends on the goal, but I don’t think it’s necessary for everyone,” she says.

What to keep in mind: Fish oil supplements can have a characteristic fishy aftertaste, so it might take some trial and error to find one that works for you (read: doesn’t leave you gagging). What’s more, absorption and bioavailability can be a challenge, according to Dr. Jordan. Because omega-3s, like vitamin D, are fat-soluble, taking fish oil with a meal that contains fat can help skirt this problem. Some claim krill oil doesn’t cause the dreaded aftertaste as much as fish oil, and evidence suggests it’s also better absorbed by the body.

How it works: Iron, a mineral, acts as an essential ingredient in hemoglobin, a protein found in your red blood cells. Without enough iron, your blood won’t be able to carry out its core task of delivering oxygen to organs and tissues, resulting in anemia.

Why some docs like it: Iron deficiency is common in women due to the loss of blood during menstruation every month. “Occasionally, despite trying my hardest to seek out iron-rich foods, I still develop an iron deficiency,” Dr. Zemtsov says. When that happens, she takes ferrous gluconate (a particular type of iron supplement) every other day to treat or prevent anemia, since research shows iron supplements are better absorbed and cause fewer side effects that way. Dr. Jordan also takes iron supplements, citing the advantages for sleep, hair health, and overall energy.

What to keep in mind: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, so pairing your iron supplement with a food that contains vitamin C or even a vitamin C supplement—as Dr. Zemtsov does—can be helpful.

How it works: Fiber, a type of carb, boosts digestion in a variety of ways: It keeps you full, helps prevent constipation, and supports bowel health. Besides the GI stuff, it also serves other functions in your body, including stabilizing your blood sugar and lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol.

Why some docs like it: “Unless you are that rare woman who regularly gets in her 25 to 30 grams per day, extra fiber intake is beneficial for almost everyone, and addresses multiple issues for me personally, including prediabetes and a rising cholesterol level,” Dr. Jordan says. She takes a fiber supplement as needed, on days when she doesn’t manage to hit her goal.

What to keep in mind: If your body isn’t acclimated to a high fiber intake, suddenly bombarding it could cause some digestive distress (think gas and bloating), so start slow to ease the transition. You’ll also need to increase your water intake simultaneously, since fiber requires water to work.

“When someone is considering a supplement, I usually recommend having a specific reason for taking it”—like a confirmed nutritional deficiency, Dr. Velayati says. “Overall, I view supplements as a way to fill a gap, not a substitute for good nutrition, sleep, exercise, and evidence-based medical care.” The bottom line: Supplements are really meant for plugging holes in your diet.

#8922. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

Last medically reviewed on August 2, 2024

#8921. Holst completes Adjaye-designed mass-timber library in Oregon

Photography by Christian Columbres

US architecture studio Holst has created a mass-timber library in Oregon, with a series of tall columns at the entrance and a central atrium, after taking over the project from Adjaye Associates.

The East County Library in Gresham features a trapezoidal roof structure on top of a mostly square building envelope, creating multi-storey covered entry programmes on each side.

These entry programmes are lined with massive glued-laminated (glulam) mass-timber columns that Holst said speak to a primary effect of the design: “awe and accessibility”.

“One of our major main vision points of the project was this idea of awe and accessibility,” Holst principal and creative director Brittany Shreiner told Dezeen.

Shreiner said that the accessible component comes from the dual entry programmes that open up to a plaza on one side, with space taken from a converted street, and an elevated entryway on the other that features ramps.

A rail line is located on one side and a bus line on the other, connecting the building to the wider public realm.

For the team, the building needed to be a “big civic moment”, thus the massive columned entryway. However, Shreiner said that the awe the studio aspired to create was more akin to that of a forest, and the mass timber helped them to express that.

Structurally, the building has a mix of concrete and mass timber elements, with mostly wooden floorplates and some walls, and concrete-and-steel cores.

The facade is a mix of vertical timber elements interspaced with high-performance concrete bands with scalloped shapes and vertical bands of glass.

At one point, a grey-toned concrete panelling system marks the semi-circular protrusion where the structure’s amphitheatre is.

The appearance of the building is close to the original design submitted by Adjaye Associates – Holst was the architect of record at the start.

However, after misconduct allegations against Adjaye Associates founder David Adjaye were made public in a Financial Times investigation, the studio was released from this project, among others. Adjaye denies the allegations.

Shriener said that the biggest changes in the design were the removal of screens that were supposed to overhang from the covered entryways and a tower that extended past the roof plane.

“There was still a lot of design to be done [at that time], but the bones of the building were there. The community buy-in was there. The stakeholder buy-in was there,” said Shriener.

“So, the county was definitely clear in their intention that they did not want to proceed with Adjaye as part of our team, and that they basically trusted us to bring the project forward, but they didn’t want to see a total redesign by any means.”

Having recently solidified itself as a name in the US mass timber game with a tall building in Portland, the studio focused on optimising the timber usage as it took over the design. It worked closely with local mass-timber supplier TimberLab for the materials.

One detail that stands out is the notches in the timber columns and beams that give the structure a cabin-like or residential appearance, while remaining monumental in scale.

More than just a style conceit, the notches play a role in the ceiling plane, hiding the mechanical systems and lighting.

Inside, vestibules compress the entry to the library, which then opens up into a main core that runs between the entrances, with a double-height atrium space in the middle, complete with a wood-slatted spiral staircase.

For Shriener, this middle space represents a “clearing” in the forest.

The primary book-storage spaces surround the main central area, with smaller breakout rooms and classrooms lying mostly on the perimeter.

Mass-timber elements remain visible throughout the interior spaces, with green carpets at times continuing the forest metaphor.

On the roof, a series of sawtooth lightwells bring diffuse light into the main central space, while a rooftop patio allows guests to enjoy the views of the mountains beyond.

Elsewhere in Oregon, Holst created a Gaudí-informed apartment building wrapped in wood.

Other projects that were completed after the fallout from the Adjaye allegations include the Princeton Art Museum, where David Adjaye “stepped back” from the project in the late stages, according to Princeton.

#8920. Are Single Older Ladies Really Happy Without Marriage? Experts Weigh In

At some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married? What if I never find my person and end up alone?

For Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office. Back then, she says, “a woman who didn’t want a husband was assumed to have something wrong with her.” But her therapist—married with children, yet more open-minded than most—didn’t try to correct her with cheesy motivational mantras or fear tactics about a “ticking clock.” Instead, she asked a different question: What kind of husband would you want, if you had one?

Joan listed a few traits. Someone busy, she recalls saying. Someone deeply absorbed in his own life—his job, his hobbies, his community.

“So you'd want someone intellectually stimulating?” her therapist asked.

“No,” Joan replied. “I’d want someone who’s never home.”

It landed as a joke, though deep down, it wasn’t. What came from that session was an almost accidental realization that sounded radical at the time (it was around 1980): “Some people genuinely live their best lives independently,” Joan tells me. Now 79, single, and uninterested in changing her relationship status, she has spent decades proving her theory true.

For much of modern history, women like Joan were cast as anomalies, freaks, or worse: cautionary tales. There’s “the childless cat lady.” The “old maid.” The “lonely spinster.” Singlehood was framed as a transitional phase, a temporary stop on the way to finding the One. Not an end goal, and certainly not a fulfilling one.

But the stigma is softening—and the older, unmarried women of this generation are living proof that a life without a husband isn’t a fallback; it’s a deeply satisfying choice.

You can see it in the collective fatigue around modern dating (78% of users on apps including Tinder, Hinge, and Bumble reported feeling burnt out, per a recent Forbes Health survey). Young adults in their mid 20s to early 30s (the supposed “prime marriage years”) are having far less sex than previous generations, with sexual inactivity up roughly 50% for women over the past decade. The shift shows up in pop culture too—in particular, the growing appetite for plots that sideline romance in favor of friendship, independence, and chosen families (like in Barbie and Wicked).

But perhaps the clearest proof is in lived experiences. The several 70-somethings I spoke with for this story have been single for decades—and aren’t wishing they’d done it any differently. If anything, their lives carry a sense of ease and expansiveness. Many describe weekly, laughter-filled girls’ nights and happy hours; solo trips planned on a whim; financial freedom to buy property, adopt pets, start small businesses…literally do whatever they want, whenever they want. A few still date casually, dipping in and out of steamy flings only when it suits them. Others have opted out of romance entirely. “My favorite part?” one 73-year-old woman tells me bluntly. “Not having to bicker or put up with an incompetent man. That’s probably why I’m the least stressed I’ve ever been.”

Across their stories, there’s no regret or hint of “missing out.” Just single older ladies enjoying where they are—nothing like the caricatures of the bitter man-hater or the desperate, unlucky romantic we’re used to seeing.

As Joan is quick to point out, “not everyone starts off wanting a romantic relationship and then moves on to singlehood as Plan B.” It’s a perspective that’s become increasingly common, so much so that sociologist Bella DePaulo, PhD, built a framework (and wrote a book) about it: being Single at Heart. These are women (including herself) who don’t end up alone; they orient toward it as a genuine preference.

“I still smile when I think about the men I dated when I was a very young adult,” Dr. DePaulo, 72, tells me. “But I remember even more fondly how I felt when each of those relationships ended: finally free.”

The practical benefits of singledom—solitude, strong friendships, fewer relational stressors—aren’t exclusive to unmarried folks. “But in my opinion, couples are never free the way single people are,” Dr. DePaulo says. The difference, she claims, is psychological: the ability to structure a day, a life, or a passing thought without reflexively factoring in another person’s needs or reactions. “A romantic partner is also there in your mind almost all the time,” Dr. DePaulo points out—even if only on the periphery. “That might be comforting for some. But it can also feel a bit unwelcome, as if they’re always considering what their significant other may be wanting or feeling.” Remove that, and your attention and energy become fully your own.

Of course, the ability to choose this lifestyle is relatively recent. For centuries, marriage wasn’t just a matter of romance—women relied on it for financial stability, social acceptance, and a sanctioned path to family, Kris Marsh, PhD, sociologist and author of The Love Jones Cohort: Single and Living Alone in the Black Middle Class, tells SELF. But with greater access to education, careers, and economic independence (along with broader definitions of intimacy, family, and fulfillment), the pressure to couple up has eased. As of 2023, 42% of US adults were unpartnered, according to the Pew Research Center (up from 29% in 1990). And among the non-daters younger than 50, half aren’t interested in a relationship—though enjoying your single status doesn’t have to involve an anti-love attitude.

“Now, a lot of women are looking for something additive,” Dr. Marsh says. “I’ve heard over and over, ‘I’m already in a very good place on my own. So you can’t be a distraction. You can’t disrupt my peace.’” Though for most, that epiphany doesn’t happen overnight.

Alice Foster, who recently turned 80, is a classic example of someone who followed the cultural script handed to many in her generation: marry young, raise children, enjoy the stability. “It was fine, but I felt like it was never really about me,” Foster tells SELF. “It wasn’t my life.”

In 1988, her marriage ended in divorce—though what followed wasn’t the loss she had been taught to fear. It was space. Peace. Recalibration. She moved upstate. Went back to school. Built a new career in nursing. Slowly, she began constructing a life that finally felt like her own.

“I feel like I’m in my 50s. It’s been so fun,” she reflects. “I love being retired. I love traveling. I love having people visit me. I love not having to answer to anybody. I’ve been single for so long and loving this life so much that, honestly, I don’t want to get tied down.” And that, experts say, is often how it works.

Rather than being a fixed moral stance or a lifelong rejection of romance, singlehood tends to be a lived, flexible experience—an acceptance of being on your own that you don’t always realize you’re choosing until later. Maybe, like Foster, you leave an unsatisfying marriage. You pull back on exhaustive online dating. You decide this is the year you’ll focus on work, hobbies, or travel. Over time, you stop planning life around the possibility of a relationship…and start seeing that you already have the joy you thought only a husband could provide.

Still, a question tends to linger: Are these women actually happy?

Recent research suggests yes—in fact, satisfaction with singlehood tends to increase with age, starting for people in their 40s. Despite cultural progress, there’s still skepticism as to why anyone would willingly stay single. Whereas married people are taken at their word when they claim fulfillment (even though we know that’s not always true), those who deviate face public scrutiny. “They have to be extra strong, exceptionally confident to stand comfortably in their singleness and validate to the world that they are, in fact, thriving,” Dr. Marsh adds—an expectation that flattens single older ladies into either a hyper-independent success story or a pitiable failure, with little room for nuance.

But that pressure can have an unintended effect too. After decades of being asked by society to justify their lifestyle, many simply stop performing. All of the women I spoke with didn’t overexplain. They weren’t defensive. They didn’t seem especially interested in winning me over.

It takes a certain kind of confidence and clarity to stop shaping your life around what’s expected and historically rewarded, and instead follow what feels good, without apology. What you get then, as Dr. Marsh has observed in her research, is a quieter, rarer form of happiness—one that isn’t performed and doesn’t ask for external validation. Instead, it feels much more genuine. It endures.
