#8907. What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

With the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one issue keeps coming up: the side effects. As important as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she says. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”

Fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen says.

You can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen says. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

Fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing issue worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen says: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

Now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation issue), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen says.

With that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen says. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

People who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we said above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen says. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”

Another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

Whatever new fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu says. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

#8906. Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research shows starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

However, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That said, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#8905. SOM unveils design for luxury waterfront development on Australian pier

International architecture studio SOM is set to transform a historic pier in Geelong, Victoria, into a waterfront destination culminating in a rounded high-rise.

SOM recently won the competition to design the 10,000-square-metre development for developers Gurner Group and Costa Property Group, which will add public space, apartments, a 200-room hotel, shops and restaurants over the water at Corio Bay.

The project will involve transforming and extending the existing Cunningham Pier, which was originally built in 1855 to give railway access to docking ships. It underwent major refurbishment in 1929, and now acts as a stretch of car parking spaces culminating in a restaurant and event space.

Envisioned as a pedestrianised waterfront destination, visitors will enter SOM’s revamped pier through a public square with water features.

A 34-storey building will rise at the end of the pier, which will surpass the 21-storey Miramar apartment tower to become Geelong’s tallest building.

Trefoil in plan, the tower’s form will resemble three combined cylinders that taper towards the top and bottom.

Lining the length of Cunningham Pier will be a series of buildings with rounded edges and layered terraces, designed by SOM to reference the movement of water and marine forms.

The luxury development will contain around 280 apartments and 12 waterfront villas with individual yacht berths.

Activity spaces and sports courts will be built on floating platforms.

SOM hopes the development will establish Cunningham Pier as “both a neighbourhood on the water and a destination for Geelong’s residents and visitors”.

“An elevated public promenade forms the organising spine of the proposal,” said SOM. “By positioning new construction alongside the historic pier, the design preserves the existing structure below while creating a pedestrian environment above.”

“Shops, restaurants, and places to gather would line the route, connecting the city to activities and views across Corio Bay.”

According to SOM, the redevelopment will involve creating new marine habitats at the pier to support biodiversity.

“This ecological ambition forms part of a broader approach that considers the waterfront as a place for both public life and marine life,” said the studio.

Other projects recently unveiled by SOM include a tiered skyscraper that rises on a waterfront site in Chicago, and plans to build a 20-storey data centre in Kansas City.

#8904. Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a new reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

The appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”

That role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”

But is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a big deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson says. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial issues that occur with age, Dr. Molina says. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”

As with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson says. It’s also extra important to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

There’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she says—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

#8903. Text Neck Exercises: Simple Moves to Ease Digital Strain

Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone. But all that screen time can lead to a pesky condition called “text neck.” Hunching over your device can leave you with some severe aches and pains.

So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!

Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.

Most of us check our phones with our heads tilted forward and down. When you do this for too long, the muscles in your neck get strained. The muscles in the back are overstretched, while the ones in the front are compressed.

If you have text neck, here’s what you might be dealing with:

But don’t get bent out of shape about overusing your favorite device. There’s no solid proof that your phone habits are to blame for your neck woes. Several studies found no connection between using your device and having neck or shoulder pain.

You could get a sore neck from overusing your muscles for many other reasons, like genetic factors, weight issues, or bad posture. “Text neck” might be a term concocted by a chiropractor to get your business. But, hey, we’re not judging.

To help ease text neck pain, try these simple exercises.

Aside from these cubicle-friendly exercises, here are some ideas to help keep text neck from being a regular pain in the y’know:

“Text neck” is the popular term for the head and neck pain caused by hunching over your device for too long. But don’t throw away your beloved device just yet. More research is needed to link “text neck” to your tech time.

In the meantime, sit up straight and do gentle exercises like neck rolls, chin tucks, and shoulder rolls. To prevent text neck from hitting you up on the reg, take regular breaks from your phone and seek out habits that help lengthen and strengthen your body. Your neck will thank you!

#8902. OEB Architects channels 1980s interiors for London extension

Glossy ceramic tiles, a glass-block wall and a leafy garden were intended to evoke tropical modernism and 1980s interiors for London Tropical, an extension to a Victorian terrace designed by local practice OEB Architects.

OEB Architects was tasked with creating an open-plan kitchen and dining space at the rear of the three-storey terrace in Southwark that would feel “surrounded” by its garden.

“The project considers how an extension to a typical Victorian outrigger can connect to its modest urban garden,” Gabriel George, project architect at the studio, told Dezeen.

“It explores the layering and overlaying of translucent and reflective materials and bold, graphic objects to give a nuanced and varied space through all seasons, contributing to a feeling of living surrounded by the garden,” he added.

Instead of filling the width of the site, OEB Architects pulled the extension back from the southern boundary, allowing it to be lined with both a glass-block wall and full-height windows that address a courtyard and side return.

This openness continues around to an end wall with full-height sliding glass doors, not only framing the garden but allowing the space to be entirely opened up to a patio surrounded by leafy planting.

“The clients were keen not to have a conventional top-lit infill extension, with a roof light sloping down to the boundary, as is common among extensions to Victorian terraces,” George told Dezeen.

“This expansion is set back from the boundary, providing both a passage and a new outlook from inside,” he continued.

“This results in two new external spaces, a courtyard addressing the main house and the rear garden serving the extension. Each is wrapped in full-height glazing with a range of transparencies responding to each view.”

The extension’s interior is defined by a kitchen island clad in glossy green tiles and a column clad in shiny red tiles, acting as spatial anchors that contrast the otherwise minimalist, white-painted surfaces, stone floors and pale timber carpentry and ceilings.

Both the glossy tiles and translucent glass-block wall were used to create a changing quality of light throughout the day, with the south-facing courtyard able to be screened off via translucent curtains that further add to this effect.

“The material and spatial ideas were driven by conversations with the clients discussing architectural precedents along with art, graphic and design references, including mid-century West Coast American case study houses, 80s interiors and tropical modernism,” George said.

The extension’s floor level steps upwards to meet the back of the main home, where the connecting corridor has been flanked by a bathroom and pantry space.

OEB Architects was founded in 2018 by directors Tessa Baird and David Eland, and has offices in London and Brighton. The studio previously completed another extension for a home in Tottenham, which expanded a semi-detached home with a simple blockwork and timber structure.

#8901. The Latest and Greatest Sunglasses for Triathletes, Tested in Training and Racing

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Sunglasses and triathletes go hand in hand. With not one but two sports calling for a good pair, and after so much time spent nitpicking over the perfect goggles, we can’t settle for less when it comes to shading our eyes through the bulk of our training and racing.

It’s not just about UV protection and keeping bugs and debris out, because, let’s be honest: style matters, too. And today’s saturated performance sunglasses market offers a nearly unlimited selection of styles, with many pairs more high-tech and often higher-priced than ever before.

We wanted to get a clearer, less-tinted picture of the triathlon-worthy sunglasses landscape in 2026, so we combed the internet to see what was on the cutting edge and spent the summer testing a wide range of pairs while running and cycling across different terrains and climates.

Along the way, we explored the latest tech, picked out standout features, and figured out what felt worth the money – and what wasn’t quite there yet. From light-shifting photochromic lenses and video-recording AI smart glasses to everyday pairs that won’t break the bank, here’s our roundup of the best sunglasses for triathletes in 2026.

In the Pacific Northwest where I live, it can be raining one minute and sunny the next. A ride might take you from wide-open roads into dense, dark forests, sometimes around a single corner. For that reason, I’ve found light-shifting lenses incredibly useful. But even if you don’t live where I do, these glasses are practical in plenty of other changing light conditions, such as an early-morning long ride that starts before the sun comes up and ends well into the day.

One of the biggest drawbacks of traditional photochromic sunglasses is that the lenses don’t always adjust as quickly as the light changes. Their tint range also has limits, and they don’t always get as clear or as dark as you’d like. Most rely on UV light to darken, which means they may not respond as you’d expect behind a UV-blocking windshield in your car or when you’re testing them by a window before heading outside.

That’s a perfect segue into where we’ll start, as the first pair on our list looks to address these issues by taking a different approach: tint you control with a swipe.

One of the most intriguing pairs on this entire list comes from a new brand called Povec. Rather than waiting for the lenses to react to changing light, these glasses allow you to swipe an interface on the temple to change the tint in about a second.

Sure enough, I was surprised by just how quickly, and how dramatically, the tint changed. It started shifting as soon as we swiped the temple, so naturally, we spent the next several days playing with it back and forth. The electrochromic tech, as it’s called, worked so well that the glasses quickly became a showpiece for impressing friends.

These glasses ironically shone in dimmer conditions, especially when we went off-road or deep into the forests and needed to change the tint quickly. When mountain biking, being able to change the tint almost immediately as we rounded a corner into a dense forest descent felt invaluable.

At the same time, we were slightly less impressed with the optical quality in harsher light. There are subtle but apparent reflections, and the clarity is just a little off. It’s nothing dramatic, but it is noticeable, especially compared with the crystal-clear optics of some other glasses on this list.

Our favorite everyday pair of photochromic sunglasses, especially for spring and fall days in the PNW forests, was the SunGod Velans 2.

This ultralight pair offered some of the best optical clarity, field of view, and comfort of any glasses on this list, even before the added bonus of photochromic lenses. They shifted from light to dark quickly enough for our normal riding, although they couldn’t match the on-demand tint changes of the Povecs.

SunGod has become increasingly visible in triathlon thanks to athletes such as Hayden Wilde and Chelsea Sodaro donning them, but also because of a few appealing extras not often found elsewhere in the market. An array of customization options, an emphasis on durability, repairability, and recycled packaging, and a lifetime guarantee that includes repairs for accidental breakage make the higher price easier to digest. Furthermore, features such as replacement lenses and screwless hinges make the price more logical and suggest this pair will likely last you for the long term rather than just a couple of seasons.

Tifosi consistently makes it into our roundups for offering quality sunglasses at some of the best prices, and its light-shifting options are no exception.

We tried the Rail XC with Clarion Blue “Fototec” lenses, which offer a stated light-transmission range of 12% to 46%.

Compared with the SunGods, these felt like only a small step down in optical quality and fit during our testing. We did notice more glare from sunlight at certain angles and slightly more fogging during humid runs. At 31 grams, they were also a little heavier.

But beyond that, there’s little else to nitpick. They’re comfortable, clear, and transition smoothly and quickly, with nose pads and temple tips that adjust on the fly, offering plenty of room to dial in comfort.

Perhaps the most controversial pair on this list, these smart glasses have divided opinions about where this technology belongs in triathlon. From Ironman banning their use at its events to T100 welcoming them through a partnership, it’s a hot topic.

After training and racing in them twice, my own mixed opinion comes down to something simpler: I thoroughly enjoy wearing them and appreciate their practicality, but I’m still struggling with the bulky styling of the Vanguard. Enough so that I often intentionally leave them behind so I’m not the guy with the video sunglasses when running or cycling with friends.

That functionality, on the other hand, is hard to argue with. Being able to capture hands-free video and photos, listen to music, take phone calls, and ask Meta questions — among many other features — makes these glasses useful in ways a regular pair simply can’t match.

The Oakley Prizm lenses offered the clarity we expected, although the bulkier frame slightly restricted the field of view. Even after keeping them in their case and using only a microfiber cloth to clean them, I also noticed tiny scratches under close inspection after a few months of use. They weren’t noticeable while wearing the glasses, but they were there.

At 66 grams, you’ll notice the weight, too. If you have one of the lightweight alternatives on this list sitting next to them, you might think twice before grabbing these for an everyday session.

Where these really earned their place is in documenting your triathlon experiences. At SOS Triathlon and Escape from Alcatraz, capturing moments before, during, and after the race felt almost effortless. I could quickly tell Meta to take a photo or record a video, then download the footage to my phone through the app afterward, and I was set. Compared with previously having to bring GoPros, set up shots, and worry about batteries and SD cards, it makes it all too easy.

On the way to the SOS check-in tent, I even asked Meta to help me remember the different stages of this unique multi-stage race (read more about the SOS here).

Like it or not, smart glasses are likely to become an increasingly familiar sight around triathletes. After using them, I can understand the appeal.

Read a full Oakley Meta Vanguard review here.

The award for the most pleasantly surprising sunglasses on this entire list goes to this Oakley Meta rival, which packed in enough features to put the Vanguard on the ropes.

I’ll admit I went into testing the Rover sunglasses with the preconceived notion that these wouldn’t compete with the powerhouse name above. But I was taken aback by both the quality and functionality.

The first things I noticed were the weight, more than 10 grams lighter than the Vanguard, and the lenses. I hadn’t expected optics this good from a brand I had never heard of.

Then it only got better. The Rovers offer both landscape and portrait recording, plus a tiltable camera that helps you adjust the shot. The video resolution was also better than I expected at 3K and 60 fps – all capabilities the Vanguard doesn’t offer.

One of the standout features was the intercom function, which lets the glasses act like a walkie-talkie with fellow cyclists using the BleeqUp app. Being able to talk to each other more easily is something I’ve always wanted on small group rides, and hearing everyone clearly through the sunglasses themselves takes away the hassle of phone calls or dealing with headphones.

They’re marketed as AI sunglasses, with tools for quickly editing captured footage and adding ride-data overlays. If you’re feeling extra AI-adventurous, you can also generate a third-person view of your ride using mapping data and an uploaded photo of yourself and your bike. The results were interesting, to say the least.

Where the Rovers fell slightly behind the Vanguards was in the polish. The interface, AI assistant, and connectivity didn’t feel as refined as Meta’s. The feedback sounds weren’t as distinct, and connecting the glasses could be a little confusing, with frequent requests to reconnect to their Wi-Fi.

The Vanguard also comes with a charging case, which simplifies things, while the Rover uses a magnetic USB charger. Finally, having to say “Hey Bleeker” to activate the assistant just felt super weird.

One final gripe: The temples could rub against the lenses when folded, which felt like a small but frustrating design oversight.

In contrast to the pleasant surprise of the BleeqUp Rovers, these heads-up display sunglasses fell well short of my expectations.

I was excited to see whether technology similar to what we’ve enjoyed in Form’s smart swim goggles could bring the same benefit to running and cycling. Unfortunately, I was disappointed from the moment I unboxed them.

The idea is great, but the execution wasn’t there. The fit was the least comfortable of any glasses on this list, sitting unusually high on my face, and the secondary inner lens that houses the HUD projection compromised the view.

The bright green data displayed on the inner lenses is intended to keep cyclists from having to look down at their bike computer so they can focus on what’s ahead. In practice, however, I found the view even more distracting, sometimes struggling to adjust my focus from what I was reading on the glasses back to the road.

It was less of an issue while running, and thankfully, you can adjust the brightness and make some changes to the display position to keep the data less intrusive, but that was little consolation.

The app also felt unfinished, and we experienced several issues trying to connect our devices. Top it off with the worst-sounding built-in speakers and most robotic voice assistants I’ve heard in a while, and I’ll sadly be leaving HUD glasses out of my periphery for a while.

If I had the budget and could choose just one everyday pair to wear everyday or bring on a trip, like our recent all-in Ironman World Championship coverage, I’d choose the Oslo 2.0.

The blend of aesthetics, lens quality, and fit is hard to beat. Grippy temple tips and a very grippy nosepiece (which comes in various sizes) help it transition easily from casual use to training. Although it doesn’t look like it’s meant for running, it performs as well as a pair designed specifically for the sport.

For cycling, though, I prefer a little more lens coverage. That’s where I’d reach for Roka’s San Remo Air, which offers a similarly understated cafe style, but with more coverage and a vented lens for hot days.

Both were pairs I could happily wear all day, and all night if I had to. They also had some of the fewest fogging issues while running in the heat and humidity of a Washington summer and felt among the most premium of the bunch — from the finish of the frames to the cases they came in.

Our favorite mid-priced everyday pair was the Adidas Kaphiros, which came surprisingly close to the Rokas in overall performance. It also became the pair my wife consistently stole – sorry, “borrowed” – before we headed out for a ride together.

These are truly glasses you forget you’re wearing. They almost feel like they float above your ears. If pressure around your ears is something that regularly bothers you — as it has for me in the past — this is the pair I’d recommend.

The lenses offer generous coverage for cycling protection, and the optical quality impressed me. Small openings in the temples let air through while riding, although the glasses tended to fog during hot, humid runs — likely due to the size of the lenses.

Tifosi makes this list for a second time, beating out plenty of other running and cycling sunglasses as our favorite budget everyday pair.

The Vogel XC is lightweight, has proved durable enough to survive a couple of seasons with me, and offers a rimless, vented design that’s hard to beat at this price.

The lens tint we tested hit a useful middle ground for the varied conditions we wore it in. And the size and shape don’t scream “I’m a triathlete” every time you wear them out in public.

#8900. Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next big thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”

The medication is currently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide users lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

“Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

But, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

If you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more important, he points out.

#8899. Inaugural Walker Design Triennial features flesh-like speakers and post-apocalyptic scenes

A set of speakers with flesh-like exteriors was among the conceptual design work shown at the first Walker Design Triennial in Minneapolis, USA, which curator Joseph Grima said reflected on the meaning of design in a world fixated on optimisation.

Filling a series of galleries at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota, the exhibition was called Beyond Materialism and featured numerous examples of conceptual design.

The pieces ranged from the historical works such as Italian radical designer Alessandro Mendini’s 1970s Lassù – paired with depictions of the performance of the chair on fire – to an international set of design studios representing the field today.

Grima, who has served as a curator and educator for several high-profile institutions including Design Academy Eindhoven and international exhibition series Alcova, said the show was meant to challenge mainstream conceptions of design.

“We live in an age that is conditioned to think that anything and everything can be designed, and often what is that everything can be optimised,” said Grima.

“And it’s precisely this association between design and optimisation that this exhibition intends to question.”

With objects of various scales on display, the Walker Design Triennial featured a room with large-scale conceptual installations. Many of the participants were international, with a cohort of contemporary US designers, including Germane Barnes and Theaster Gates.

Terracotta plinths were included as part of the exhibition design, supporting many of the small and large objects.

Some of the pieces were commissioned directly for the event, mainly in the large-scale section.

Among these was Spanish designer Lucas Muñoz Muñoz’s All Ears, a set of latex-covered speakers that were programmed to play sounds recorded in the months before in Minneapolis. A sleek soundboard allowed users to play the tracks, with multiple tracks routed through the amorphous, fleshy speakers all at once to cacophonic effect.

Muñoz told Dezeen that the installation was designed to be a “microphone” for the city itself and “make visible the act of listening”.

The broadcast from the soundboard was also projected out of the gallery as a radio sequence.

Also commissioned for the event was a work by Vessel, featuring two massive rolls of fabric spooled over a kiosk. The fabric was based on Vessel cofounder Navine G Dossos’s paintings of her and her partner James Bridle’s self-built home.

Also in the large-scale room was a series of post-apocalyptic appliances made from found objects by Brussels-based Espace Aygo, derived from the studio’s 2022 transformation of a derelict apartment building into a home and art space.

The themes of fleshy objects, post-apocalypticism, and reuse continued into the rooms with smaller objects.

Here, London-based studio Superflux showcased objects from its Relics of Abundance series, showing objects created by a future civilisation that may someday use our objects today in a time of scarcity, including a chair made from straw and rebar.

Austro-Canadian designer Christoph Wimmer Ruelland created a series of furniture pieces with found objects that are extraordinarily colour-matched, while Korean designer Jonghoo Jeong utilised jerrycans to create a fountain, a reference to his past practice of dumping the objects in his process.

Athens-based studio Astronauts showcased inflated metal works informed by the autobody shops, creating love seats, chairs and even a seesaw that are iridescent while still familiar.

Italian-German designer Maximilian Marchesani created a structural piece made of smartphone glass that refracts metal-coated leaves as well as a chandelier that combined LEDs with branches. South Korean studio Wknd Lab created a series of stools made from discarded shells.

Dozens of other designers took part in the installation, including Moon Seop Seo, Studio Ker, Objects of Common Interest, Stef Fusani, Kevin Quale and Kostas Lambridis, representing a who’s who of avant-garde design, refracted through the lens of Grima and the event’s artistic director, Asli Altay.

It was an “opportunity to stop, take stock for a moment, and reflect on what design is today,” said Grima.

Other recent design showcases include a show of wood furniture by Armadillo and furniture made from fragments of New York buildings by Rafael Prieto.

Beyond Materialism is on show at the Walker Art Center from 17 October 2026 to 14 February 2027. Find out more about design and architecture exhibitions, talks and fairs at Dezeen Events Guide.

#8898. Bumps Inside Nose: Common Causes and Top Treatments

There are many possible causes for bumps inside your nose — some as harmless as a pimple, others that might need more attention. It’s easy to imagine the worst, but the truth is usually less alarming.

If you’ve got a painful, annoying, or strange bump in your nose, keep reading to learn what it might be, whether it’s worth worrying about, and how to deal with it.

So, what’s behind these bothersome nose bumps? Here are some common culprits:

This is inflammation of the nasal vestibule, the area just inside your nostrils, often caused by bacterial infections. It can lead to painful, red bumps sensitive to the touch. Common triggers include frequent nose-picking, blowing too hard, or even plucking nose hairs.

Like on your face, the pores inside your nose can become clogged with oil, dirt, and bacteria, leading to pimples. These can be painful and may swell, especially in such a sensitive area.

Non-cancerous growths can develop in the nasal passages or sinus lining due to chronic inflammation, allergies, or infections. While they’re usually painless, larger polyps can cause blockages, leading to breathing difficulties, a reduced sense of smell, or recurrent sinus infections.

When you pluck or trim nose hairs, the hair can sometimes grow back into the skin instead of out, causing an ingrown hair. If this becomes infected, it can result in a painful bump inside the nose.

A bump can also form inside the nose due to trauma, such as a blow to the nose, or even from something as simple as aggressive nose-picking. The trauma can cause the tissue to swell or become bruised. In some cases, a hard bump may form as the tissue heals.

Fluid-filled sacs that can form in your nose, usually harmless but sometimes uncomfortable.

A hard bump inside the nose might be due to problems with the cartilage, such as a deviated septum or cartilage overgrowth.

Small, benign bumps that may appear on or in the nose are often mistaken for pimples but are fibrous tissue growths.

Wondering if that bump inside your nose is something serious? Here’s what to look out for:

Ready to say goodbye to that pesky bump inside your nose? The proper treatment depends on what’s causing it, but here are some ideas to ease the discomfort and promote healing:

Additionally, if you’re dealing with nasal polyps, a healthcare professional might prescribe steroid sprays to shrink them and reduce inflammation, making breathing easier.

On the other hand, if a bacterial infection is the culprit, as in cases of nasal vestibulitis, your doc may recommend a topical antibiotic like mupirocin. This ointment is applied directly inside the nose to target the infection, reduce redness, and promote healing.

While most nose bumps aren’t a big deal, some need more attention. Here’s when to make that appointment:

Even the slightest bump inside your nose can be a major annoyance. Causes vary from harmless pimples to things that require more attention, like polyps.

Self-care measures can usually ease discomfort and speed healing, but if it’s super painful or worrying discharge, it’s time to sniff out professional help.

#8895. Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

It’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But new research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

“These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

The research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

The researchers discovered that while participants said they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

“We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”

Ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh says. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”

People are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

As a result, Dr. Gallagher says she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”

These chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

“Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen says. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a big impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen says.

Over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan says. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

Of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan says. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”

Ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she says. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”

#8893. Ontario house by Brian O'Brian takes cues from farm buildings

Canadian architect Brian O’Brian has completed a rural weekend house in Ontario that features a slanted, corrugated-metal facade and an angled roof covered with greenery.

The Hemlock House sits on a 72-acre (29-hectare) property in the southern town of Markdale.

The project grew in scope over time. Originally, the plan was to renovate an old farmhouse, but the client ultimately decided to create an entirely new house.

“What started as a modest renovation evolved into a full replacement of the small, 1930s farmhouse,” said Brian O’Brian, a Toronto-based architect.

The commission came about after the client saw another project by O’Brian in the area – a 19th-century schoolhouse with stone walls that had been converted into a cottage.

For the Hemlock House, O’Brian took cues from the region’s agrarian buildings to conceive the design.

Set on a flat site surrounded by woods and farmland, the house is composed of a long bar and adjoining box, and totals 3,250 square feet (302 square metres).

A long entry driveway “traces the lineage of the site”, passing by an old farmhouse and century-old barn.

The new house draws upon these earlier buildings and “extends the language of agricultural buildings into a contemporary domestic form”, the architect said.

The home’s bar-shaped volume is topped with a sloped, metal-clad roof, while the attached box has an angular green roof.

The north side of the house is lined with a slanted wall made of corrugated metal.

Cut into the wall are three windows, which can be covered by external, perforated steel panels that slide up and down. This elevation also features a boxy protrusion with wood cladding.

“This is meant to feel like an agrarian building at first view, but one that begins softening and opening on approach,” said the architect.

The southern elevation – which overlooks patios and a swimming pool – features hemlock siding and ample glazing. Various roof overhangs help shield the building from sun and snow.

The house also has a carport, which is sheltered by a canopy made of wood and metal.

Within the home, there is a division between public and private spaces.

The linear volume, which spans two levels, contains a principal suite, a secondary suite, and two bedrooms with a shared bathroom. The adjoining box holds a kitchen, dining area and living room.

Rooms feature neutral colours and a mix of earthy and industrial materials.

“Concrete and hemlock define every surface, carrying a steady material logic through the house,” the architect said.

Other projects in Ontario include a 1970s chalet that was renovated and expanded by UUfie to conform to its steep site, and a black cabin by Barbora Vokac Taylor that includes wedge-shaped clerestory windows.

#8892. The Swedish Sport of Swimrun Is Spreading Across the U.S. I Tried It and Chaos Ensued.

Outside features editor Frederick Dreier participated in the October 4 Ötillö Swimrun race at Horsetooth Reservoir, Colorado. Dreier has competed in triathlons, bicycle races, and other endurance sports for 25 years.

A few memories come to mind from my recent Ötillö Swimrun, the endurance race that combines open-water swimming with trail running.

In one, I flounder in the chilly waters of Colorado’s Horsetooth Reservoir near Fort Collins, my arms feeling heavy as concrete as I struggle to swim in a straight line. In another, I sit by the side of a rocky trail plucking cactus spines out of my backside, moments after a clumsy toe-strike sent me tumbling into a clump of prickly pear.

Both of these scenes, however, are superseded by a memory with an altogether different vibe. That, of course, is crossing the finish line and exchanging a flurry of high-fives and hugs with a bunch of random sweaty strangers, all of us clad in wetsuits, goggles, and running shoes.

You see, I had a blast racing my first Ötillö Swimrun race despite the dead-tired arms and cactus butt.

If you have never heard of the swimrun racing format, here’s a quick primer. Picture a triathlon, minus the biking. Now, chop up the swimming and running portions, stitch them together in smaller portions, and spread the whole event out on a point-to-point course. You run, then swim, then run again, then swim, and so on. The event I did was a “sprint” distance event, comprised of five swims and six runs spread out across 12 miles of trails and lake.

It took me nearly three hours to complete, and at no point was I sprinting.

Unlike triathlon, where you abandon your gear after each portion, swimrun requires you to carry all of your stuff from start to finish. Thus, you must swim while wearing your running shoes, run while clad in your wetsuit, and carry your pull buoy, hand paddles — swimming gear that is allowed — for the entire journey. This makes for some hilarious blunders along the way (more on this later).

Within the swimrun world, Ötillö is the proverbial Ironman — the most recognizable brand of events. Outside has a somewhat rich history of chronicling the Swedish company, first in 2013, then in 2014, and also in a 2017 Brad Stulberg column. In 2019, longtime contributor W. Hodding Carter wrote an Outside feature story about his foibles at the Ötillö world series race in Cannes, France, where he and his partner paddled across the green-blue Mediterranean and jogged through the French Riviera.

In all of those stories, Ötillö swimrun races come across as grueling, fun, and distinctly European. The racing format, after all, was developed in Sweden and first held on the chain of islands just east of Stockholm, which is still the site of the annual Ötillö world championships. The name “Ötillö” is a Swedish word that loosely translates to “island to island.”

Good news for Americans: Ötillö is no longer just for the Euros. In 2023, the series expanded to North America after it purchased a budding collection of U.S. swimrun races called the Odyssey series, that were co-founded by a guy named Lars Finanger. Finanger and I were roommates in Boulder 20 years ago, back when we were both dirtbag triathletes chasing a daily endorphin high.

Now, Finanger is trying to spread the Swedish swimrun gospel in the U.S., where jogging trails while wearing a wetsuit is about as popular as pickled herring.

“We started out with a lot of triathletes, Ironman finishers, Eco-Challenge racers — it was a really eclectic group of endurance athletes,” Finanger told me. “Now we have a small but dedicated following of athletes who see themselves as Swimrunners first, even though they might do a triathlon or a bike race, too.”

Finanger first learned about Ötillö from the 2013 Outside story. He was burned out on triathlon and road bike racing and was looking for a new challenge, so he signed up for the world championship event in Stockholm, which is comprised of 38 miles of running and 5.7 miles of swimming, and requires participants to compete in teams of two. It’s a grueling test of endurance and grit that takes many teams upwards of 10 hours to complete.

“I had this big grin on my face throughout the whole thing, even though the water was so frickin’ cold and the trails made you feel like you were running through the hobbit scene from Lord of the Rings,” Finanger told me. “I realized we didn’t have anything like it in the USA.”

Finanger wanted to start his own race but didn’t know how. As luck would have it, he wasn’t the only person intrigued by the format. Jeffrey Cole, a veteran of the endurance sports industry and a longtime triathlon race director, emailed Finanger about the swimrun format. Cole said that Casco Bay, Maine, near his home in Kennebunkport, was a perfect place to recreate the island hopping of Sweden’s Ötillö. In 2016, they started the inaugural Odyssey event along the Maine coast.

“I think about the history of triathlon, where athletes raced in Kona and then went back home to put on their own races where they lived,” Finanger said. “We wanted to produce a swimrun that we’d have wanted to do ourselves.”

Their model was a success. Finanger and Cole started other swimrun races in the U.S.: Orcas Island, Washington; Cedarville, Michigan; Austin, Texas; and even one on California’s Catalina Island. These events are held annually, and the participation numbers now surpass 400 at some races.

Cole died in 2018, and Finanger kept the business going alongside a handful of new partners. In 2023, Ötillö approached them about purchasing the Odyssey series and bringing it under the corporate umbrella. Finanger said it was a no-brainer.

“It meant partnering with the gold standard in our sport,” he said.

These days, the former Odyssey races award points to elite athletes that help them qualify for the world championships race in Stockholm. But they also boast shorter distances, solo categories, and a laid-back vibe. Because the purpose of the events, Finanger told me, is to attract newbies like yours truly to the format.

“We are still this meeting ground for all of these different types of athletes — swimmers, cyclists, triathletes,” he said. “The one they have in common is they are adventure-minded.”

Qualifying for a race in Europe was not on my mind as I prepared for the 2026 Colorado Ötillö. The shorter sprint distance did not offer qualification points toward the Ötillö World Championship; however, the much longer World Series race in Colorado (23 total miles) did.

When I asked Finanger for strategic advice, he just laughed me off. “Just have fun out there, dude,” he said. He reminded me that the whole point was to have a personal adventure while swimming and jogging my way around the lake.

The laid-back atmosphere at the start line reinforced Finanger’s advice. Over the years, I’ve nervously waited for the start of Ironman triathlons, marathons, and almost every type of bike race out there. At Ötillö, the vibe was extremely chill — like what you’d expect at the start of a 5K color run or a boozy bicycle parade and not a three- to five-hour test of stamina.

Still, I had to remind myself to have fun more than a few times during the early moments of the race. Following a fast one-mile run to start the race, we plunged into Horsetooth Reservoir for the first swim.

I’m a former NCAA Division III swimmer and multiple Ironman finisher, and I’m accustomed to swimming in choppy water filled with thrashing arms and legs. But I struggled to find my groove with the swimrun gear, and I had to stop a few times to position my pull buoy between my legs and learn to swim while wearing sneakers. An even bigger challenge hit when I exited the water.

I stepped onto the clay beach and immediately stumbled around like a newborn fawn. I felt like I’d just gulped a tequila shot or three. I lumbered toward the trail and zigzagged my way up a hill like a punch-drunk boxer.

Upon exiting the water, seasoned swimrunners fastened their pull buoys to their waists with a cord, tucking the apparatus to their lumbar sections like a fanny pack. I fumbled to secure mine as I trotted along, the buoy bouncing off of my butt. As I twisted and twirled the buoy, one of my plastic swim paddles slipped from my hand, and I heard it crash into a bush. Should I stop to look or keep going? I wondered. I chose to stop.

The short pause allowed my thumping heart rate to chill. Soon, my brain fog cleared, and I was able to focus. I found the paddle, and as I jogged along the trail, I familiarized myself with the goofy gear. I practiced tucking and untucking my pull buoy into its tether. I threaded the fingers of my right hand through the elastic loops on my hand paddles to keep them secure.

During a triathlon, you’re constantly using products that are over-engineered for the specific modality of the moment: aerodynamic bike stuff, cushioned shoes, high-visibility swim goggles. Part of the fun quirk of a swimrun is learning to manage the wrong gear when it’s not used for the right job.

My confidence increased, and I picked up the pace, jogging past swimrunners and moving to the side as others jogged past me. People seemed stoked to be on the trail. Nobody seemed so caught up in their own struggles as to skip the customary “Lookin’ good!” or “Go get ’em!” during a pass.

The sprint course deviated from the World Series route near the five-mile mark, and I bid adieu to the athletes who were tackling the longer distance. I saw a handful of sprint racers up ahead of me and decided to push my pace on a long switchback ascent to try and catch them.

Perhaps it was my soaring body temperature inside my wetsuit, or my lingering buzz. But as I closed in on the guy ahead of me, my mind wandered, and I tripped on a rock, completed a somersault, and landed in the cactus. Bewildered, I made a mental note about swimrun: shit can hit the fan if you don’t pay attention.

The fall meant that I had to spend a few minutes plucking spines from my backside once I crossed the line. But the ordeal delivered one of my lasting takeaways from the race.

Perfection does not exist during a swimrun. Even during a shorter distance race, you’re bound to inhale water, drop your gear, battle through exhaustion, or trip and stumble. How you deal with these setbacks defines your experience out there.

I’ve spent the last 25 years trying out different endurance sports. And I’m familiar with the progression that most athletes follow with these sports. You try out a sport and fall in love with the adventure, camaraderie, and community. Then, as the years go by, you focus more on your results, and before you know it, you’re completing a training regimen, following a performance-oriented diet, and dreaming of a top-10 finish.

I will absolutely compete in another Ötillö Swimrun event, but I don’t envision myself ever getting too hardcore about the format. Simply doing a swimrun gave me enough feeling of adventure and carefree silliness, without an ounce of self-seriousness. Sucking at the format provided half of the joy. And I’m more than happy to chase that feeling again.

British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. #8890. Rucking Benefits: Add Weight to Your Walk to Boost Fitness and Strength

Weightlifting isn’t the only way to build muscle. Rucking, or walking with a weighted backpack, is also highly effective. It’s easy to start, can be done anywhere, and helps build muscle, burn fat, and boost endurance.

Curious? Keep reading to discover why rucking might become your new favorite workout!

Rucking is like taking your regular walk and cranking up the intensity with heavy cargo. It’s as simple as strapping on a weighted backpack (aka rucksack) and hitting the pavement, the trail, or wherever you like to roam. Originally dreamed up by the military to toughen up soldiers, rucking, or a rucksack march has, er, marched into civilian life as a killer workout.

What makes it awesome? The extra weight transforms a casual stroll into a workout that means business. Plus, it’s customizable — you can load up as much or as little weight as you want, making it perfect for any fitness level. And the best part is that you can ruck just about anywhere.

Rucking isn’t just a walk in the park — it’s a powerful workout that packs a punch in all the right places. Here’s why rucking deserves a spot in your fitness routine:

Think of rucking as the ultimate multitasker for your body. It’s like lifting weights but with cardio to keep your heart pumping.

As you lug that weighted backpack around, your legs, back, and core are putting in serious work, building strength, and endurance with every (weighted) step.

Want to torch calories without the treadmill monotony? Rucking’s got you covered. The extra weight and steady movement combo turns your stroll into a calorie-burning machine. Perfect for shedding any additional pounds while keeping things interesting.

Carrying a weighted backpack helps your posture. Your core has to stay engaged to keep you balanced, which helps align your body and ward off injury.

If you’ve had a baby, rucking can be a game-changer, helping combat the postural shifts of pregnancy and hauling around kids. Plus, it builds the functional strength you need for everyday life, like lifting groceries or wrangling toddlers.

Rucking easily fits into a busy schedule. You don’t need special equipment beyond a sturdy backpack or a gym membership, and you can do it while multitasking — think walking the dog in the morning or pushing a stroller. Plus, the whole family can join in, making it a great way to combine fitness with family time.

Starting rucking is easy, but here are some tips to help you get the most out of your rucks:

Rucking is generally safe, but here’s how to stay injury-free:

Yes, rucking can help build muscle, especially in your legs, core, and back. The added weight provides resistance, similar to strength training.

Start with 10 to 15% of your body weight and adjust based on your comfort and fitness level. Heavier weights can affect your balance and stance, making injuries more likely. As you progress, you can gradually increase the weight.

Yes. Rucking forces your upper back and shoulder muscles to step up, giving your traps a solid workout as you carry the weight.

Ruck yes! Rucking is a low-impact, full-body workout that kicks butt.

Tell your boring walk on the treadmill to ruck off and trade it in for a waltz about with a weighted rucksack. Rucking could be the secret sauce your fitness routine has been missing, helping you build muscle, shed pounds, or get those steps in.
